records.title: UV-B irradiation disrupts obligate endosymbioses and reduces fitness in agricultural pest insects
records.abstract: Abstract    Sap-sucking insect pests, such as aphids and whiteflies, depend on obligate bacterial endosymbionts for survival. Driven by evolutionary genome reduction, these symbionts often lose essential DNA repair pathways, potentially leaving them defenseless against UV-induced damage—a vulnerability that remains untested as a pest control strategy. Here, we evaluated ultraviolet-B (UV-B) efficacy against three strawberry pests (  Chaetosiphon fragaefolii  ,  Aphis gossypii  , and  Bemisia tabaci  ) and linked host susceptibility to symbiont DNA repair capacities. UV-B irradiation significantly reduced pest survival and fecundity, with  B. tabaci  exhibiting extreme susceptibility even at low intensity. In  B. tabaci  and  C. fragaefolii  , UV-B depleted primary endosymbiont titers (  Portiera  and  Buchnera  ), disrupted bacteriome morphogenesis, and impaired oocyte development. Comparative genomics, including a newly assembled  Buchnera  genome, confirmed that all examined obligate symbionts had lost most dark-repair pathways, with  Portiera  lacking almost all repair mechanisms. This repair-gene erosion extends to obligate symbionts of other major agricultural and medical pests. Our findings demonstrate that UV-B impairs pest fitness by exploiting DNA repair-deficient obligate endosymbionts, establishing a novel paradigm for pest management that targets the evolutionary 'Achilles’ heel' of insect endosymbiosis.
records.authors: Tsuchida T, Fujita S, Kuroda R, Kurosawa K, Nagahashi M, Ootaka H, Yamamoto T, Ochi T, Fujiwara A.

records.title: Intracanal administration of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis HN019 modulates the microbiota of periapical lesions in male rats.
records.abstract: ObjectiveThe oral microbiome comprises a complex microbial community that plays a fundamental role in maintaining oral health by preventing the proliferation of pathogenic microorganisms. This study aimed to investigate whether the probiotic strain Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis HN019 (B. lactis HN019) can modulate the microbiota associated with periapical lesions.DesignThirty-one Wistar rats were randomly allocated into four groups (n = 8/group): healthy teeth; periapical lesion infection; periapical lesion treated with vehicle (2% carboxymethylcellulose [CMC]); and periapical lesion treated with a probiotic solution containing 2.7 × 10⁹ CFU of B. lactis HN019 in 2% CMC. On days 7 and 14 after infection, 600 μL of vehicle or probiotic solution was applied in root canal orifice and aspirated, followed by placement of 5 μL inside the root canal before restoration. After euthanasia, hemimandibles were processed for histological analysis. Laser capture microdissection was used to isolate periapical lesion samples for DNA extraction and bacterial identification by 16S rRNA sequencing. Alpha diversity was analyzed using one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests (5% significance).ResultsHealthy teeth exhibited a characteristic resident microbiota, with Staphylococcus aureus, Cutibacterium acnes, and Streptococcus oralis as the most abundant species. In the infection group, Streptococcus agalactiae predominated. In the probiotic group, Streptococcus agalactiae and Bacteroides fragilis remained predominant, while Lactobacillus reuteri significantly increased compared with the infection group (p = 0.033).ConclusionB. lactis HN019 modulated the microbiota associated with periapical lesions, supporting its potential as an adjunctive strategy to promote microbial balance and tissue recovery.

records.title: Marker-Centered Evaluation of De Novo Assemblers Using Validated Microsatellite Loci in the Endangered Korean Fish Pseudopungtungia nigra.
records.abstract: The recovery of experimentally validated microsatellite loci from short-read assemblies may provide an application-specific measure of assembly quality that complements conventional genome-wide statistics. In this study, four de novo assemblers-SPAdes, ABySS, SOAPdenovo2, and MaSuRCA-were evaluated using genomic reads from two individuals of the endangered Korean freshwater fish Pseudopungtungia nigra. Assembler performance was assessed based on assembly contiguity, BUSCO completeness, computational requirements, and the recovery of 20 PCR-validated microsatellite loci and their flanking regions. SPAdes produced the most contiguous assemblies and the highest BUSCO completeness among the tested assemblers, with N50 values of 5.5-7.0 kb and BUSCO completeness of 30.2-35.2%, and recovered all 20 loci and their flanking sequences at high confidence in both individuals. Marker recovery by ABySS, SOAPdenovo2, and MaSuRCA varied according to k-mer size and sample, with high-confidence recovery decreasing at larger k-mer sizes in several configurations and reaching 9 of 20 loci in the least favorable condition. SPAdes used 32.1-34.2 GB of peak memory, compared with up to 135.0 GB in the most memory-intensive SOAPdenovo2 runs. Reference-guided comparisons retained substantially greater total aligned sequence with the two Pseudorasbora references than with the more divergent Cyprinus carpio reference, although the mean identity of the smaller retained C. carpio alignment set was slightly higher. All 20 validated marker sequences produced high-confidence provisional placements in both Pseudorasbora reference genomes. As an exploratory downstream application, the SUC6832-derived pseudo-reference enabled joint genotyping of the two samples and yielded 2,012,643 filtered candidate variants across 25 guide-assigned scaffolds. These results indicate that SPAdes provided the most favorable balance of validated marker recovery, relative assembly quality, and memory efficiency among the tested configurations, although all assemblies remained fragmented at the genome-wide level. Marker-centered benchmarking can therefore complement conventional assembly statistics when short-read assemblies are generated primarily for microsatellite development, while pseudo-reference-based genomic analyses should remain provisional because of assembly fragmentation, reference bias, and limited biological sampling.

records.title: Integrated profiling of β-lactam susceptibility and spoilage-associated enzyme activities in psychrotrophic bacteria from the raw milk production chain.
records.abstract: Psychrotrophic bacteria are important targets for microbiological control of cold-chain raw milk because of their ability to produce spoilage-associated enzymes and harbor antimicrobial resistance determinants. However, these two functional characteristics are often investigated separately, leaving their co-occurrence within the same isolate collection insufficiently characterized. To address this gap, 543 dominant culturable bacterial isolates were recovered from raw milk and dairy-farm-associated samples collected from six regions of China. Pseudomonas was the most prevalent genus, followed by Acinetobacter, Chryseobacterium, Serratia, and Psychrobacter. β-Lactam minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) distributions varied substantially among genera, with Chryseobacterium exhibiting the highest proportion of β-lactamase-associated phenotype-positive isolates. Among 226 raw-milk isolates screened using ceftazidime, all 44 isolates showing inhibitor-responsive or carbapenemase-associated phenotypes were subjected to whole-genome sequencing. Genome-wide resistance-gene screening identified annotated β-lactamase genes predominantly in Chryseobacterium and Acinetobacter. In contrast, the resistance-related annotations retained in phenotype-positive Pseudomonas isolates were mainly associated with efflux systems and adaptive response mechanisms. In the integrated analysis, a relative MIC-enzyme risk-prioritization score ranked Serratia (0.88), Chryseobacterium (0.71), and Pseudomonas (0.67) as the three highest-ranking genera. The β-lactam MIC score showed weak positive correlations with the protease-associated score (Spearman's ρ = 0.297, P < 0.001) and with the lipase-associated score (ρ = 0.194, P < 0.001). These findings indicate that genus abundance alone is insufficient to characterize the functional heterogeneity of psychrotrophic bacteria in raw milk. Integrating β-lactam MIC patterns with spoilage-enzyme activity provides complementary information for genus-level prioritization within this isolate collection.

records.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. IMPORTANCE  Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire  Orthohantavirus genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection.

records.title: Genetic code expansion enables plant-directed control of bacterial activity.
records.abstract: Microorganisms have the potential to deliver growth-promoting benefits to plants and crops; however, to be useful in a field setting, their gene expression should be programmable and restricted to specific plant hosts and conditions. Here, using O-methyl-L-tyrosine (OMY) as a model compound, we establish noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) as a tool for plant-based control of associated microbial activity. We use genetic code expansion to engineer OMY-dependent control of protein synthesis in the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis. Engineered B. subtilis strains express an orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and tRNA pair that, upon provision of OMY, results in suppression of in-frame amber stop codons in target transcripts. We engineer Arabidopsis, tomato and poplar to biosynthesize OMY, showing that plant-derived OMY can stimulate gene expression in both model and wild soil bacteria. This demonstrates that inducible and tissue-specific expression of a single biosynthetic enzyme by the plant enables on-demand control over microbial activity, establishing ncAAs as a tool for programming plant-microorganism partnerships.
records.authors: Zhong V, Jones MA, Cabales A, Gevorgyan A, Inckemann R, Johnson AA, Karunadasa SS, Forti AM, Xu SL, Kunjapur AM, Brophy JAN.

records.title: Host-like temperature unlocks glucose uptake and metabolism in pathogenic Leptospira.
records.abstract: Pathogenic Leptospira transitions between environmental reservoirs and mammalian hosts, exposing the bacterium to distinct temperature conditions. Although Leptospira is generally considered to rely primarily on long-chain fatty acids for growth and to have limited capacity to use glucose, whether host-like temperature alters glucose-associated metabolic capacity remains unclear. Here, we used transcriptome-integrated genome-scale metabolic modeling to examine temperature-dependent metabolic states in pathogenic Leptospira. Models contextualized with transcriptomic data from cultures at 37°C predicted increased flux through glucose transport, glucose phosphorylation, and downstream glucose-associated reactions than it did at 29-30°C. Similar temperature-dependent predictions were obtained for another pathogenic Leptospira species under in vitro conditions. Consistent with these findings, analysis of leptospires cultivated intraperitoneally in dialysis membrane chambers also predicted enhanced glucose uptake and metabolism under host-temperature conditions. In vitro validation experiments showed increased bacterial uptake or accumulation of a fluorescent glucose analog, elevated expression of candidate glucose transporter genes, and glucose-dependent enhancement of bacterial growth at 37°C. Treatment with a glucose degradation pathway inhibitor, 2-deoxy-d-glucose, further supported a contribution of glucose-associated processes to proliferation at 37°C. Together, these findings indicate that pathogenic Leptospira displays condition-dependent glucose uptake and glucose-associated metabolic activity that become apparent at host-like temperature, as opposed to being glucose-incompetent at environmental-like temperature. This prediction-driven framework refines the conventional view of Leptospira carbon metabolism and provides a basis for future studies of glucose-associated metabolic capacity during mammalian infection.ImportanceEnvironmental reservoirs play a central role in the transmission of many bacterial pathogens, yet the metabolic mechanisms that enable adaptation to both environmental and host-associated niches remain largely unknown. Using a prediction-driven framework that combines contextualized genome-scale metabolic modeling with multi-omics analyses and experimental validation, we discovered that pathogenic Leptospira activates glucose uptake and metabolism only under host-like conditions. This finding resolves a long-standing misconception arising from studies performed under conventional laboratory conditions and fundamentally revises our understanding of Leptospira physiology. More importantly, our study establishes an integrative systems biology strategy for uncovering condition-dependent metabolic traits that would be difficult to identify experimentally alone, with broad applicability to diverse environmentally transmitted pathogens.
records.authors: Ozuru R, Yoshimura M, Powers DA, Sonoda T, Papin JA, Obata F, Kolling GL, Hiromatsu K.

records.title: Host genetics structure Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages and their co-variation in sympatric fire coral species
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  Host genetic and environmental filtering are key determinants of microbiome assembly, yet their relative influence across multiple symbiotic compartments remains poorly understood. In coral holobionts, studies typically focus on either algal or bacterial symbionts and rarely account for host genetic variation below the species level. Here, we combined host microsatellite genotyping with ITS2 and 16S rRNA metabarcoding to investigate the drivers of Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages in three sympatric fire coral species (  Millepora cf.  exaesa ,  M. tenera , and  M. cf.  platyphylla ) across three adjacent but environmentally contrasting reef habitats on Réunion Island. Both symbiont assemblages were structured by host identity and habitat, although host genetics consistently outweighed environmental effects on the microbiome composition. At the subspecies level, host genotypes explained up to 54% of the variation in Symbiodiniaceae assemblages compared to 20% for the prokaryotes. Symbiodiniaceae communities were dominated by  Symbiodinium A16 and A3 radiations, while showing marked specificity across species and habitats. All  Millepora species consistently associated with the Spirochaetaceae, Kiloniellaceae and Desulfobacteraceae bacterial families across all habitats, suggesting evolutionarily maintained core associations. Integrative analysis further demonstrated genotype-specific co-variation between algal and bacterial symbionts, with some genotypes maintaining stable and co-varying symbionts across clones, while others exhibited more flexible assemblages. Together, our results indicate that sympatric fire coral acquire symbionts from locally available pools through host genotype-dependent filtering. This study highlights host genotype as a major determinant of coral holobiont assembly, shaping the composition and co-variation of both Symbiodiniaceae and prokaryotic assemblages.
records.authors: Pozas-Schacre C, Derome N, Boissin E, Mercière A, Martineau G, Mercier P, Bourmaud CA, Dubé CE.

records.title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis in adrenoleukodystrophy: a new piece in the puzzle?
records.abstract: ABSTRACT  X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is the most common monogenic disorder affecting brain white matter, presenting a broad clinical spectrum from slowly progressive adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN) to rapidly advancing cerebral demyelination. Factors influencing the variable disease expressivity remain poorly understood. We conducted shotgun metagenomic profiling of fecal samples from X-ALD patients and integrated these data with targeted plasma metabolomic analyses of amino acids and key metabolic intermediates. We identified distinct microbiome-associated metabolic signatures across X-ALD phenotypes. Notably,  Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and  Helicobacter apodemus abundance were significantly altered in AMN compared with childhood CALD patients. In parallel, X-ALD patients exhibited evidence of microbial metabolic remodeling characterized by altered amino acid metabolism, reduced folate biosynthetic potential, and enrichment of stress-adaptive pathways, including redox-associated functions, glyoxylate shunt activity, lipid A modification, lipopolysaccharide assembly, biofilm adhesin biosynthesis, and curli fiber production. Consistent with these microbial changes, plasma levels of branched-chain amino acids and methionine, as well as serum folate concentrations, were significantly reduced. Importantly, methionine levels showed an inverse correlation with neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentrations in patients with cerebral disease. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between gut microbial metabolic capacity and systemic metabolic alterations in X-ALD. Our results reinforce previous evidence implicating methionine metabolism in disease severity. Collectively, these data support a modulatory role of the microbiota–gut–brain axis in neuroinflammatory and mitochondrial-related processes underlying X-ALD progression and highlight new opportunities for biomarker development and microbiome-informed therapeutic interventions.

records.title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
records.abstract: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.
records.authors: Cao X, Wang Y, Sun H, Feng R, Zhang H, Li Y, Lee H, Karaahmet B, Li B, Gersbach C, Crawford GE, Taga M, Beeri MS, Buchman AS, Klein H, De Jager P, Bennett DA, The Alzheimer's Disease Functional Genomics Consortium, Wang G, Dey KK.

records.title: Identification and characterization of new P. aeruginosa phages using a surface receptor platform
records.abstract: Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined  Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of  P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.
records.authors: Tran VN, Lahane TS, Qaderi I, Harvey H, Burrows LL.

records.title: cpr0186 contributes to promoting sporulation in Clostridium perfringens SM101.
records.abstract: ObjectivesAlthough the precise mechanism underlying activation of Spo0A needs to be clarified to fully understand C. perfringens sporulation, the molecules directly interacting with Spo0A have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to identify proteins interacting with Spo0A during C. perfringens sporulation by a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assay.MethodsPrey libraries constructed using the genomes of C. perfringens SM101 and str. 13 and a bait plasmid encoding the receiver domain of Spo0A in C. perfringens SM101 were used for Y2H assay. The deletion mutant and its complemented strain were constructed by homologous recombination. Phenotypic analyses included measurements of bacterial growth, sporulation efficiency, cell morphology, mRNA expression of sporulation-related genes, and the amount of phosphorylated Spo0A. Potential protein interactions were evaluated using AlphaFold 3.ResultsY2H screening identified CPR0186, a hypothetical protein in C. perfringens SM101, as a Spo0A-interacting candidate, and AlphaFold 3 modeling supported the possibility of the direct interaction with the receiver domain of Spo0A. The cpr0186-null mutant exhibited growth comparable to that of the wild-type strain, but showed significantly reduced sporulation. The mutant also showed significantly decreased mRNA expression of spo0A, sigF, sigE, sigG, and sigK. No apparent difference in the ratio of Spo0A∼P to unphosphorylated Spo0A was observed among the strains under the conditions tested.Conclusioncpr0186 promotes sporulation in C. perfringens SM101 and is suggested to contribute to the expression of Spo0A-regulated genes. CPR0186 may interact directly with Spo0A although the functional significance of this interaction remains to be determined.
records.authors: Yasugi M, Sugimoto M, Kusakabe S, Miyake M, Nariya H.

records.title: Aniline Biodegradation and Nitrogen Removal by Salt-Tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1: Performance and Potential Mechanisms of Catechol-Mediated Enhancement.
records.abstract: Industrial wastewater containing salts, nitrogen, and aromatic pollutants presents challenges for biological treatment. Although salt-tolerant microorganisms have shown potential for nitrogen removal and aromatic pollutant degradation, their functional versatility and the effects of co-substrates on pollutant biodegradation remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigated the aniline degradation and nitrogen removal capabilities of salt-tolerant Pseudomonas sp. H1, with particular emphasis on catechol-mediated enhancement of aniline biodegradation. Strain H1 degraded only 9.11% of aniline (200 mg⋅L-1) within 60 h as sole substrate, but the degradation rate approached 100% within 24 h with catechol as co-substrate. Moreover, the strain tolerated high salinity (20-60 g⋅L-1 NaCl), achieving a maximum average NH4+-N removal rate of 10.98 mg⋅L-1⋅h-1. Whole-genome sequencing, nitrogen balance analysis, and enzyme activity assays supported ammonium assimilation as an important nitrogen removal pathway. Transcriptomic analysis revealed differential expression of genes associated with antioxidant defense, carbon metabolism, and aromatic compound degradation under catechol-supplemented conditions, suggesting potential transcriptional responses associated with enhanced aniline biodegradation. These findings demonstrate that catechol supplementation can substantially improve aniline biodegradation by a salt-tolerant bacterium with nitrogen removal capability, providing a basis for the potential application of strain H1 in saline wastewater treatment.
records.authors: Zha Z, Ren Y, Chen F, Yu C, Lei L, Li Z, Chen H.

records.title: Efficacy of Two Antimicrobial Peptides Against Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae in Kiwifruit.
records.abstract: Kiwifruit bacterial canker caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa), has led to substantial economic losses worldwide and represents a major challenge to kiwifruit cultivation. Due to the inadequate effectiveness and environmental safety of current treatments, there is a pressing demand for novel antimicrobial compounds, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). In this study, two AMPs, P255 and P256, previously designed by our group, were used to determine their efficacy against Psa in kiwifruit. P256 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 18.75 µg/mL demonstrated stronger antimicrobial activity against Psa than did P255. P256 and P255 showed synergistic effect when combined with EDTA. In addition, they effectively inhibited the biofilm formation, and regulated the expression of genes related to Psa biofilm formation. Both peptides bound with the lipopolysaccharide of Psa, targeted the membrane and increased the permeability of Psa cell membrane, resulting in calcium leakage. P256 and P255 disrupted the cellular morphology and intracellular structure of Psa cells. They also bound to the genomic DNA of Psa and induced the accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species. In experiments on infected leaf discs, P256 and P255 displayed superior control of Psa compared to commercial agricultural streptomycin. Collectively, P256 and P255 efficiently controlled Psa in kiwifruit and could be further developed as a new eco-friendly bactericidal agents.
records.authors: Zhou Y, Yang Y, Wang L, Gao Y, Xu X, Ying F, Dang X.

records.title: First contact: biophysical insights into non-enveloped viruses from VLPs to packed virions.
records.abstract: Precise biophysical characterization of non-enveloped viruses and virus-like particles (VLPs) is essential for evaluating assembly, structural integrity, and sample heterogeneity - key parameters that influence infectivity, manufacturability, and therapeutic performance. Analytical ultracentrifugation, light scattering, and mass photometry provide complementary information on particle size distributions, empty/full ratios, and assembly quality. Native and charge-detection mass spectrometry extend this, enabling accurate mass determination and genome-loading assessment. Solution-based structural techniques, such as SAXS and spectroscopy, provide dynamics. High-resolution X-ray crystallography, cryogenic electron microscopy, and tomography reveal global architectures, quaternary arrangements, and conformational switching essential for entry and maturation. Besides these methods, atomic force microscopy also allows nanoscale visualization in conjunction with mechanical profiling, linking physical stability with functional behavior. Thermal, chemical, and mechanical stress assays offer insight into unfolding pathways, pH-dependent disassembly, and genome-driven capsid pressurization, informing both viral biology and formulation science. Finally, mass spectrometry-based methods enable site-specific mapping of post-translational modifications and conformational perturbations. Together, these approaches establish a comprehensive framework for characterizing viral particles and VLPs, supporting rational engineering of stable, homogeneous, and functional assemblies for vaccines, gene delivery, and nanobiotechnology. This review summarizes current label-free methods for assessing size, mass, structural organization, and stability of intact viral particles.
records.authors: Rothe J, Uetrecht C.

records.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
records.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.
records.authors: Gurer-Er DC, Karakulah G, Gautheret D, Akgul B.

records.title: Foodborne Bacterial Protein Toxins: Structural Genomics, Stability, and Prospects for Enzymatic Detoxification in Food and Gut Environments.
records.abstract: Foodborne bacterial toxins remain a major global health threat, causing millions of diarrheal cases annually by disrupting ion balance, inhibiting protein synthesis, and dysregulating immune responses. Key agents include AB5 enterotoxins such as cholera toxin, heat-labile toxin, and Shiga toxins; heat-stable peptides (STa/STb); staphylococcal superantigens; and pore-forming toxins from Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens. Encoded on mobile genetic elements or chromosomal loci, these structurally robust toxins often resist host proteolysis, limiting natural detoxification. Despite abundant data on individual toxins, an integrated synthesis that links high-resolution structural and genetic features with practical implications for enzymatic neutralization is lacking. This review addresses this gap by compiling the structural genomics of major toxin families and mapping toxin architecture and gene context onto stability profiles and enzymatic vulnerability. We examine their genetic organization, structural stability, and susceptibility to enzymatic neutralization by microbial proteases, probiotic-mediated modulation, and engineered biocatalysts. Enzymatic detoxification of mycotoxins is discussed only as a limited translational analogy: small-molecule conversion by lactonases, oxidoreductases, or hydrolases is biochemically distinct from proteolysis of large, conformationally complex protein toxins. Thus, mycotoxin studies inform enzyme-discovery and engineering workflows but do not constitute direct evidence that these pathways can neutralize AB5 holotoxins, superantigens, or pore-forming toxins.
records.authors: Pham THH, Nguyen TL.

records.title: Borrelia-specific cell-free DNA in plasma from adults with Lyme neuroborreliosis: an explorative study.
records.abstract: Current blood-based diagnostic modalities for LNB have significant limitations. Using Next Generation Sequencing, we investigated blood samples from patients with LNB and non-LNB controls for Borrelia burgdorferi-specific cfDNA (Bb-cfDNA). Blood-samples from 61 adults suspected for LNB were analysed with amplification-free Nanopore metagenomic sequencing and detected cfDNA was cross-referenced with human and Bb-genome databases to identify Bb-specific-cfDNA. Bb-cfDNA was detected in 3 of 45 patients with LNB (6.7%) and in none of the 16 controls. Positive samples contained low levels of Borrelia-classified reads. Bb-cfDNA is unlikely to become a relevant blood-based diagnostic test for LNB in immunocompetent adults.

records.title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources.
records.abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.
records.authors: Beltrán-Sauceda HA, Aguirre-Sánchez JR, Medrano-Félix JA, González-López I, Ibarra-Rodríguez A, Castro-Del Campo N, Chaidez-Quiroz C, Castro-Del Campo N.

records.title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
records.abstract: The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families

records.title: Application of metagenomic sequencing to improve sessile serrated lesion detection using the faecal immunochemical test
records.abstract: Most population colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programs use the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), which quantifies occult haemoglobin in faeces and has proven to be effective in detecting and reducing CRC incidence and mortality. Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) account for up to 30% of sporadic CRC, yet FIT has low sensitivity to detect them. Faecal microbial biomarkers may improve their detection, but FIT samples have not previously been used to study the SSL microbiome. We asked whether FIT samples preserve the faecal microbiome as accurately as fresh collection, and whether they can reveal a microbial signature of SSL. We first reanalysed a published dataset of paired FIT and fresh faecal samples from the same participants. Donor identity explained 63.5% of compositional variance compared with 16.7% for collection method, indicating that FIT preserves the donor-specific signature on which biomarker discovery depends. We then generated shotgun metagenomes from FIT samples of 24 adults scheduled for diagnostic colonoscopy, twelve with at least one clinically significant SSL and twelve with no neoplasia (NN) and compared each group with a published fresh faeces cohort matched on colonoscopy outcome. Collection method explained 6.3% to 7.6% of variance, and no individual species was significantly differentially abundant between methods. Between SSL and NN FIT samples, community structure did not significantly differ, and conservative differential abundance analysis returned no results. More permissive count-based models suggested a depletion of fermentative commensals in SSL. Functionally, SSL samples encoded significantly fewer KEGG orthologs and less polyamine biosynthesis capacity, while orthologs carried by several Bifidobacterium species were more abundant. Many depleted functions reflected Enterobacteriaceae gene content concentrated in a few control samples. No single feature was diagnostic on its own. A multi-feature signature, confirmed in larger cohorts and applied to samples that screening programs already collect, may increase the detection rate of SSLs.
records.authors: Hart BJ, Laven-Law G, Harker CM, Doane MP, Parker R, Menberu M, Cock C, Edwards RA, Symonds EL, Winter JM, Roach MJ.

records.title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
records.abstract: Background:  Residual barcode-like sequences after preprocessing are a quality-control concern in multiplexed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing data, particularly in low-biomass, host-dominated samples such as blood. Using blood datasets spiked with a microbial mock community and prepared with the Native Barcoding Kit 96 V14 (SQK-NBD114.96), we compared Dorado 1.1.1, Dorado 2.0.0, and Barbell 0.3.2. Results Dorado demultiplexing reduced barcode-positive reads to approximately 2% of reads, with internal barcode-like matches in 0.17-0.19% of reads. Barbell 0.3.2 applied to untrimmed Dorado basecalls yielded an approximately 50-fold lower detector-defined internal-match rate (0.0035-0.0037%) while retaining 91.2-91.8% of input reads. In the NCBI core_nt release of 12 September 2026, the focused screen identified complete, ungapped 24 nt identity for 64 of the 96 barcodes (66.7%), comprising 505 distinct barcode-accession pairs across 482 accessions and 195 exported TaxID groups of mixed taxonomic ranks. Records annotated as rRNA genes, chromosomes/genomes, and plasmids accounted for 35.6%, 23.2%, and 22.4% of the pairs, respectively. The barcode was located within its native ligation flanks in 224 pairs (44.4%), including 170 (33.7%) with the complete Dorado barcode search window and 3 (0.6%) with the full adapter construct. Conclusion Barbell combined 91-92% read retention with lower detected internal barcode signals. After demultiplexing, barcode-like sequences remained in sample data. Moreover, kit barcode sequences, often within their native ligation flanks, were detected in reference records. Both findings call for careful preprocessing, reference inspection, and downstream validation. Further research should determine whether barcode-associated artifacts in reads and reference records affect taxonomic classification in clinical metagenomic workflows.
records.authors: Dinse T, Englaender VR, Metz S, Schrezenmeier H, Messerer DAC.

records.title: Visual surfaceomics reveals the substrate-scavenging cell surface of Asgard archaea
records.abstract: The emergence of eukaryotes from Asgard archaeal ancestors likely required a specialized cell envelope that enabled sustained physical and metabolic interactions with proto-mitochondrial symbionts. While the protrusion-rich cell architecture of Asgard archaea may enable such interactions, the molecular composition of their cell surface and its role in establishing cell-cell contacts remains unknown.  Here, we developed a "visual surfaceomics" approach, integrating subtomogram averaging, predictive structural modeling, transcriptomics, proteomics, and expansion microscopy to identify surface proteins in situ. We show that Asgard cell bodies and protrusions lack an archaea-typical paracrystalline S-layer and are instead decorated by two main classes of surface proteins: subtilisin-like serine proteases (SubSs) and oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppAs). SubSs were detected as membrane-anchored dimers and were sparsely distributed across the surface. OppAs showed near-total membrane coverage but lacked any rigid, higher order assembly. Thermal shift assays and single particle cryo-EM showed that OppA binds oligopeptides in vitro. Comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics suggest that this peptidophilic surface architecture is conserved across Asgard archaeal phyla. Finally, we discovered that the cell surface was remodeled at cell-cell contact sites.  Altogether, our integrative approach revealed a metabolically specialized and structurally flexible cell surface that couples extracellular protein degradation with peptide capture and uptake, while potentially contributing to establishing and maintaining the symbiotic interactions of Asgard archaea.
records.authors: Malit JJL, Amendola D, Xu J, Dufresne L, Kokhanovska A, Gonet A, Wiegand CP, Clavien J, Wollweber F, Pilhofer M.

records.title: Primary vitamin B  12  limitation and widespread stress in Antarctic phytoplankton
records.abstract: Iron is considered the dominant limiting or colimiting nutrient for phytoplankton growth in the Southern Ocean. However, strong competition and limited biosynthesis capabilities for vitamin B  12 (cobalamin) within the microbial community creates conditions suitable for cobalamin limitation. Through a nutrient enrichment experiment in the Amundsen Sea, we show that growth in a phytoplankton community comprising diatoms and prasinophytes was limited primarily by cobalamin and secondarily by iron. Protein biomarkers across a broad area of the Southern Ocean further indicate widespread cobalamin stress within diatoms and  Phaeocystis . As warming-induced melting of ice-shelves increases iron supplies in the coastal Southern Ocean, shifts from iron to cobalamin limitation favor mixotrophic flagellates with low cobalamin requirements, altering community composition and function.
records.authors: Lampe RH, Rao D, Kell RM, Chmiel RJ, Schanke NL, Kim SY, Lees LE, Bolinesi F, Mangoni O, Casotti R, Balestra C, Zheng H, Moran DM, Allen AE, McIlvin MR, DiTullio GR, Saito MA.

records.title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
records.abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 μm pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.
records.authors: Bohutskyi P, Johnson Z, Velickovic M, Kim Y, Cheung M.

records.title: Temporal changes in genetic variation during the invasion of Lygodium japonicum in North America
records.abstract: Premise of the study. Invasive species are now widespread and have detrimental ecological and economic impacts. They also offer opportunities to investigate rapid evolution in colonizing populations. Here, we leverage nuclear DNA from herbarium specimens of Lygodium japonicum, an invasive fern to 1) identify the putative source(s) of its invasion, 2) test for climate adaptation in its invaded range, and 3) characterize the effects of genetic bottlenecks on adaptive and neutral variation during its establishment. Methods. We use low-coverage genome skimming data from specimens spanning 1905 through 2017 to identify the source region(s) of the L. japonicum invasion of North America. We use a genotype-environment analysis of invaded range samples to identify genomic regions associated with local adaptation to variation in five bioclimatic variables. Finally, we compare heterozygosity between native and invasive individuals and their changes through time in non-coding, coding, and putatively adaptive loci. Key results. We identify mainland Asia as the most likely source region for this invasion. Our genotype-environment analysis found 144 candidate SNPs significantly associated with climatic variation in the invaded range, with precipitation of the driest month associated with the greatest number of SNPs, suggesting rapid genomic adaptation in the invaded range. Finally, we found conflicting trends in individual-level heterozygosity over time when analyzing different types of genetic variation: in non-coding loci, there was a small, yet significant decrease in genetic diversity, but in putatively adaptive loci we did not find evidence of a genetic bottleneck. Conclusions. Natural history collections provide exceptional opportunities to explore evolutionary processes, by capturing genomic sequences across time. Here, herbarium specimens reveal rapid evolution, maintenance of adaptative variation, and accumulation of noncoding diversity in the Lygodium japonicum invasion, highlighting the potential for adaptative variation to fuel the success of invasive species.
records.authors: Pelosi JA, Pearse AR, Northing PC, Markley M, Altergott E, Beck JB, Dlugosch KM.

records.title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
records.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.
records.authors: Kara M, Ashyralyyev A, Alkan C.

records.title: Evolutionary dynamics of the pan-centromere architecture in oaks
records.abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation and genome stability, yet their DNA evolves rapidly, presenting a long-standing centromere paradox. Here we characterise the genomic and epigenomic architecture of >1,300 candidate centromeres from 111 high-quality Quercus (oak) genomes. We show that lineage-specific expansion of QuCEN146 satellite drives centromere turnover in oaks by displacing ancestral LTR-rich sequences into flanking regions, with genetic drift facilitating fixation of satellite-rich centromeres. Population-scale analyses in Q. serrata reveal extensive variation in satellite rich centromeres, generated by array expansion and contraction, strand-orientation shifts, and interspecific introgression. By contrast, LTR rich centromeres of Q. variabilis exhibit extremely low polymorphism and high collinearity across populations, sustained by suppressed local recombination, linked selection, and constrained LTR dynamics. We further demonstrate chromosome-independent evolutionary patterns for both satellite-rich and LTR-rich centromeres. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how evolutionary processes drive centromere turnover and shape contrasting centromeric sequence landscapes in forest trees.

records.title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
records.abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.
records.authors: De A, Roy A, Mondal A.

records.title: The Geography of Speciation Across Andean-Centred Clades
records.abstract: Aim:  Mountains harbour a disproportionate share of global biodiversity, yet the geographic pathways through which this diversity arises remain debated. In the Andes, diversification has been linked both to geographic isolation generated by complex topography and climatic dynamics, and to ecological divergence across steep environmental gradients. Here, we assess the predominant geographic modes of speciation across Andean-centred clades using a large-scale comparative framework, while evaluating how alternative representations of species distributions influence macroevolutionary inference. Location: Andes, South America. Taxon: A total of 102 Andean-centred genera of animals, plants, and fungi. Methods: We combined time-calibrated phylogenies with species distribution data derived from two alternative spatial representations: concave polygons and potential distribution models. For each genus, we estimated 13 summary metrics capturing range overlap, range asymmetry, and phylogenetic structure. We then used simulation-trained, likelihood-free classification approaches, including linear discriminant analysis and two approximate Bayesian computation methods, to assign each clade to its most probable geographic mode of speciation: vicariant, peripatric, parapatric, sympatric, or mixed geographic scenarios. Results: Across clades, overlap-associated scenarios, corresponding to parapatric or sympatric classifications, were inferred as predominant in 57–67% of genera, whereas strictly allopatric scenarios, that is, vicariant or peripatric speciation, accounted for 23–30%, depending on the spatial representation and classification method used. Sympatric scenarios alone were inferred in 38–52% of genera, particularly when potential distribution models were used. At least one-third of clades showed congruent classifications across both analytical methods and spatial representations. However, several genera were sensitive to how species distributions were represented, with some shifting between allopatric and sympatric classifications depending on the spatial input used. Main Conclusions: Our results suggest that Andean diversification has not followed a single dominant geographic pathway, but instead reflects a mosaic of spatial contexts involving both isolation-driven and overlap-associated scenarios. However, classifications as parapatric or sympatric should be interpreted as hypotheses of geographic overlap during lineage divergence, rather than as direct evidence of speciation with gene flow. By shifting from single-clade case studies to a broad multi-taxon comparative perspective, this study suggests that the geography of Andean speciation reflects a heterogeneous process shaped by multiple spatial pathways to lineage divergence, while identifying candidate clades for future phylogeographic, ecological, cytogenetic, and population genomic studies of mountain biodiversity.
records.authors: Ramos Torres A, Molina-Henao YF.

records.title: Acquire and rewire: mobile genetic elements co-opt the bacterial core genome
records.abstract: It is assumed that bacterial genomes are streamlined, with genes encoding core functions integrated with one another and with aligned fitness interests. Such genes can gain little from horizontal transfer, as any recipient would already carry its own copy better adapted to resident networks. These restrictions motivated the ‘complexity hypothesis’, which predicts that core genes are rarely transferred. Yet homologues of core genes are repeatedly found outside their native chromosomal context, carried by mobile genetic elements such as plasmids and phage-plasmids, and by domesticated replicons such as chromids. Explaining this pattern requires us to ask whether a copy rides a mobile, self-interested element or a domesticated, host-aligned one. On domesticated, vertically inherited carriers, a second copy plausibly serves the host, through dosage, niche-specific benefit or functional specialization. On mobile, selfish elements, it may instead serve the element, by promoting behaviors that favor onward transmission. Because they enter cells that already have a host-encoded copy, we propose that mobile variants can act through dosage or through effects disproportionate to their abundance, for example by co-assembling with the chromosomal product. Here, we discuss the evolutionary drivers and consequences of extrachromosomal core genes and argue that these overlooked copies deserve systematic study.
records.authors: Carvalho R, Hall J, Botelho J.

records.title: Discovery of Apis mellifera filamentous virus in the blue orchard bee: Characterization of impacts and interactions with an organosilicone surfactant
records.abstract: Abstract    While RNA viruses have received attention in impacts on bee health, research is limited for DNA viruses. DNA viruses, such as  Apis mellifera filamentous virus  (AmFV), have been identified in solitary bees; but infection dynamics and impacts are not well studied. We detected AmFV in diapausing  Osmia lignaria  adults and dead larvae from wild populations using metagenomic sequencing. Finding AmFV in diapausing adults in cocoons indicated an active AmFV infection. Unmodified larval provisions from nests had significant levels of AmFV, suggesting virus transmission may occur via fecal/oral routes via pollen. Using established rearing methods, we fed  O. lignaria  larvae AmFV and monitored survival, development, and adult weight metrics. Increased amounts of AmFV in larval provisions resulted in increased mortality. Co-exposure to an organosilicone surfactant (OSS) in provisions synergistically increased AmFV titers in larvae and adults, indicating that agrochemicals could affect viral infections. With increased development time from 2nd instar to pupation, bees of both sexes weighed more; however, male and female bees were impacted differently by AmFV and OSS. OSS plus AmFV exposure significantly increased the time to pupation in female bees. Male bees exposed to OSS weighed more. These results provide crucial insights into AmFV disease dynamics.
records.authors: Williams MF, Schaeffer RN, Cox-Foster DL.

records.title: Sex influences the mosquito virome in a host-specific way.
records.abstract: Mosquitoes harbor diverse eukaryotic viruses. These viral communities, or viromes, probably influence mosquito physiology, including pathogen transmission. However, the factors shaping the virome remain largely unstudied, limiting our understanding of its role in mosquito biology. Here, we assess the influence of sex on the eukaryotic virome of mosquitoes. Ecological differences between males and females, such as female-specific blood feeding, may lead to differential viral exposure and virome structure. We investigated the influence of sex in sympatric populations of Culex quinquefasciatus and Aedes aegypti, two major human pathogen vectors. A total of 5,743 mosquitoes were collected in various habitats in Burkina Faso (West Africa) over 2 years. Shotgun sequencing of 115 pools revealed 47 viral taxonomic units (VTUs) from 28 viral families. Viromes differed between the two mosquito species, enabling within-species analysis of sex effects. Significant differences in beta diversity were observed between sexes in both species, while alpha diversity differences were significant only in C. quinquefasciatus. Additionally, five indicator viruses, taxonomically diverse and including two novel species, were identified associated with sex. Most indicator VTUs were found in both sexes but with different infection rates. Their low prevalence suggests that sex-based differences are not present in all individuals but are detectable at the population level. Our findings unveil that sex can influence the mosquito virome, and that this effect depends on mosquito species. Moreover, our results provide a first model of the virome structure as a function of sex in two mosquito species of public health significance.IMPORTANCEMosquitoes carry many viruses that do not infect humans but can influence how mosquitoes interact with pathogens that threaten human health. Yet, the factors that shape these viral communities in nature remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether male and female mosquitoes differ in the viruses they carry. Sex could affect the virome because males and females have distinct ecological and physiological traits, such as blood feeding in females. We examined the viromes of two major disease vectors, Aedes aegypti and Culex quinquefasciatus, collected in large numbers in Burkina Faso and screened using metagenomics. We found that males and females harbor different viral communities, and that these differences vary between species. These patterns were not driven by sex-specific viruses but by viruses that differed in prevalence between sexes. Our findings show that sex influences mosquito viromes in the field and offer new insight into mosquito-virus interactions.
records.authors: Morel C, Gil P, Kaboré DPA, Exbrayat A, Charriat F, Soma DD, Sawadogo SP, Ouédraogo GA, Van de Perre P, Baldet T, Dabiré RK, Gutierrez S.

records.title: Bridging generalizability and reproducibility in machine learning-based antimicrobial resistance prediction.
records.abstract: The rapid growth of whole-genome sequencing and machine learning (ML) has led to a multitude of methods for predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from bacterial genomic data. Despite increasingly high reported predictive performance, substantial differences in data sets, phenotype definitions, genomic preprocessing, evaluation strategies, and validation procedures make it difficult to determine whether models will perform reliably beyond the data on which they were developed. In machine learning, this problem is generally framed in terms of generalizability: the ability of a model to maintain performance when applied to previously unseen data. In microbiology, many of the same considerations ultimately manifest as a problem of reproducibility. In this review, we provide a brief overview of the fundamental concepts underlying machine learning-based AMR prediction and then examine the factors that affect model generalizability and reproducibility.
records.authors: Elseifi N, Rogers H, Ferraro M, Boucher C.

records.title: Industrialization restructures the domestic dog gut microbiome while preserving host specificity.
records.abstract: Industrialization has reshaped human gut microbiomes, but its effects on other human-associated mammals remain poorly understood. Domestic dogs provide an informative comparative system because they have shared human environments and food systems for millennia yet retain distinct host biology. However, most canine microbiome studies have focused on industrialized companion, colony, or controlled-feeding dogs, limiting our understanding of the ecological range of the domestic dog gut microbiome. We analyzed fecal 16S rRNA gene profiles from 261 dogs sampled across Nepal, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles; 257 dogs remained after excluding those with reported recent antibiotic exposure. Lifestyle was the strongest measured correlate of canine gut bacterial composition, and this association persisted in restricted analyses of mature, non-shelter dogs sampled from temperate regions. Industrialized dogs differed from non-industrialized dogs through directional genus-level shifts, prevalence-defined VANISH-like and BloSSUM-like bacterial guilds, coabundance structure, and shifts in predicted functional potential. Non-industrialized dogs were not microbiologically uniform: pastoralist dogs showed non-industrialized gut bacterial community profiles but diverged from a simple forager-to-industrialized continuum. Cross-species comparisons with humans sampled across matched lifestyle categories showed parallel lifestyle-associated restructuring in both hosts, but host species remained the dominant axis of variation, and genus-level responses were largely host specific. These findings expand the ecological baseline for canine gut bacterial communities and identify industrialization-associated lifestyle change as a major axis of gut bacterial community restructuring in a long-term human-associated mammal. More broadly, they show that shared lifestyle transitions can impose parallel ecological pressures across host species without overriding host-specific community assembly.ImportanceDomestic dogs are one of the closest animal companions of humans, yet we know surprisingly little about how their gut microbiomes vary outside industrialized pet populations. This study shows that industrialization-associated lifestyle change is not only relevant to human microbiomes but also a broader ecological force that reshapes gut microbial communities in animals living alongside us. By comparing dogs across diverse human lifestyles, we show that shared environments can impose parallel pressures on the gut bacterial communities of humans and dogs, while each host maintains a distinct microbial identity. These findings suggest that gut microbial communities are shaped by the interaction between host biology and changing ecological conditions. Expanding microbiome research beyond industrialized settings is therefore essential for understanding what microbial diversity has been retained, altered, or lost during recent lifestyle transitions.

records.title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections.
records.abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii, and were frequently associated with off-panel blaOXA-23 detected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in Acinetobacter baumannii. However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.
records.authors: Nitayanon P, Phoonthong S, Peizner MT, Kraipasspong S, Kamolvit W, Tansirichaiya S.

records.title: From Genomics to Diagnostics: Combating the Spread of Vascular Streak Dieback in North America.
records.abstract: Vascular streak dieback (VSD) has emerged as a major threat to woody ornamental production in the United States (U.S.), currently affecting at least 50 tree and shrub species across 25 botanical genera in at least twelve U.S. states. The putative causal agent, here termed the VSD-associated Ceratobasidiaceae lineage (Csp), presents diagnostic challenges due to its fastidious growth requirements and vascular colonization pattern. Here, we integrate genomics-guided marker discovery with multi-platform genome-anchored tools (SSR, TaqMan qPCR, and LAMP that target unique genomic regions identified through comparative genomics) to deliver a field-deployable, genome-anchored toolkit for detection and genotyping of Csp across nurseries and landscapes. We evaluated the performance of these tools using 103 samples representing DNA isolated from 64 VSD-symptomatic plants or their fungal isolates and 39 non-target Ceratobasidiaceae outgroups. Genome assembly of Illumina reads yielded ten informative microsatellite markers with an overall amplification success rate of 95.8% (91.7%-100.0% across Csp samples). These markers demonstrated strong performance in distinguishing the Csp samples from the outgroups. Among the three TaqMan probes developed, VSD048 exhibited superior performance with 100% detection across Csp samples, characterized by cycle threshold (CT) values of 26.8 ± 4.2, and no cross-reactivity with C. theobromae or other Ceratobasidiaceae species. A multi-laboratory ring trial confirmed the reproducibility of the VSD048 TaqMan assay across various testing platforms. The loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the Csp-unique region achieved a sensitivity of 0.82 [95% CI 0.68-0.968] and specificity of 1.00 [95% CI 1.00-1.00], with a practical detection threshold of approximately 25 copies of the target region. Our molecular survey of the disease revealed a surprisingly broad host range beyond Cercis canadensis (Eastern redbud), encompassing eight additional genera, and confirmed its geographical distribution across the eastern and midwestern U.S. These validated molecular tools provide rapid, sensitive, and specific detection methods for Csp surveillance and management. The field-applicable LAMP assay and laboratory-based TaqMan/SSR protocols offer complementary approaches for different diagnostic scenarios, thereby enabling early detection and supporting efforts to limit the spread of this emerging pathogen in nursery and landscape settings.

records.title: Evaluation of ITS copy number variation among Clarireedia jacksonii isolates using single-copy genetic markers cam and hsp60.
records.abstract: Molecular tools are widely used for plant pathogen detection and quantification. Recent quantitative PCR applications for the turfgrass disease causal agent Clarireedia jacksonii were developed targeting the ITS region and showed potential utility in improved disease management. However, accurate and consistent pathogen quantification is contingent on stable copy numbers of the target genes across populations. In this study, we evaluated the genomic copy number of molecular markers in C. jacksonii using in silico analyses, quantitative PCR, and digital PCR. Calmodulin (cam), elongation factor 1-alpha (ef1α), and minichromosome maintenance protein 7 (mcm7) were consistently identified as single-copy loci, whereas ITS exhibited multiple copies in two out of nine assemblies. Digital PCR confirmed that cam and heat shock protein 60 (hsp60) closely followed theoretical single-copy expectations across a genomic DNA dilution series of C. jacksonii isolate HRS10. In the analysis of 27 C. jacksonii isolates, ITS was consistently detected as a multicopy locus, with copy number estimates ranging from 33 to 48 copies per genome when normalized using cam and from 34 to 52 copies per genome when normalized using hsp60. These results demonstrate that ITS copy number variation among C. jacksonii isolates was consistently observed, independent of the single-copy reference locus used for normalization. Therefore, single-copy genetic markers, such as cam and hsp60, may represent superior choices for accurate and stable estimation of fungal genome equivalents in C. jacksonii.
