records.title: Total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves improve sleep quality in mice with perimenopausal insomnia and are associated with altered expression of 5-HT<sub>1A</sub>R, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2.
records.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceHemerocallis citrina Baroni has a long history of dietary and medicinal use in China. Its dried whole herb is documented as an ethnic medicinal material in the 2003 edition of the Guizhou Provincial Quality Standards for Chinese Medicinal and Ethnic Medicinal Materials, while Hemerocallis flowers are traditionally used for "ye shao an mei" (), referring to reduced or disturbed sleep at night. Modern studies have demonstrated sleep-improving effects of the flowers, and previous work showed neuroprotective and antidepressant-like activities of total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves (HLTP). However, the effects of HLTP on perimenopausal insomnia (PMI) remain unclear.Aim of the studyTo evaluate the effects of HLTP on sleep disturbances in mice exhibiting perimenopausal and insomnia-like features and investigate associated molecular changes.Materials and methodsHLTP was prepared using a previously reported procedure. Network pharmacology predicted candidate targets and pathways for 32 phenolic constituents identified in an earlier HLTP batch, while molecular docking assessed predicted binding to 10 core targets selected by protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis. A composite mouse model was generated using 4-vinylcyclohexene dioxide (VCD) to induce perimenopausal features, followed by para-chloro-DL-phenylalanine (PCPA) to induce insomnia-like disturbances. Seventy female C57BL/6J mice were randomized into seven groups (n = 10 per group): Control, Con + HLTP, Model, HLTP-L/M/H (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, respectively), and zopiclone. Treatment began with model induction. Behavioral tests, pentobarbital-induced sleep testing, 24 h electroencephalographic/electromyographic (EEG/EMG) polysomnography, histopathology, biochemical assays, and Western blotting were used to evaluate pharmacological effects and associated molecular changes. 16S rRNA sequencing, serum untargeted metabolomics, and brain transcriptomics were additionally performed to characterize complementary changes in the gut microbiota, systemic metabolism, and central gene expression.ResultsNetwork pharmacology prioritized the serotonergic synapse pathway for further investigation. HLTP improved behavioral and sleep-related abnormalities, with the most consistent effects at the high dose. EEG/EMG polysomnography showed a partial shift in sleep-wake distribution toward the Control pattern. During the inactive phase, high-dose HLTP shortened non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep latencies, reduced Wake bout number and NREM-to-Wake transitions, prolonged NREM bout duration, and increased NREM sleep time (P 1AR) and gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor α2 subunit (GABRA2), together with decreased expression of adenylyl cyclase 5 (ADCY5) and protein kinase A (PKA) after HLTP treatment. Multi-omics analyses revealed changes in gut microbial composition, serum metabolism, and brain gene expression following HLTP treatment. Pathway enrichment analysis of exploratory candidate metabolites identified FDR-supported enrichment of steroid biosynthesis. Brain transcriptomics identified FDR-supported enrichment of circadian rhythm in the Model vs. Control comparison and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction in the HLTP-H vs. Model comparison. None of the tested cross-omics correlations remained significant after FDR correction.ConclusionsHLTP ameliorated sleep disturbances in mice subjected to the VCD + PCPA composite model, accompanied by improvements in neuroendocrine indicators and changes in 5-HT1AR, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2 protein expression. The omics findings provided complementary exploratory evidence, although the functional relationships among these changes remain to be established.
records.authors: Zhang Z, Wang Y, Meng Y, Liu J, Shao Y, Jing Y, Liang W, Li Y, Cui F, Li Y, Shao Y, Hu F.

records.title: Designing for success in early-phase hemophilia clinical trials: historical lessons and emerging principles for next-generation therapeutics.
records.abstract: IntroductionHemophilia drug development has progressed through five therapeutic eras: plasma-derived concentrates, recombinant proteins, extended-half-life molecules, non-factor rebalancing agents, and gene therapy. Each transition depended not only on molecular innovation but also on early-phase trials that addressed critical translational and safety questions before pivotal testing.Areas coveredThis review examines the evolution of early-phase hemophilia trial design across these five eras, identifies lessons from successful and unsuccessful programs, and proposes a ten-domain framework encompassing translational science, population selection, dose-finding, endpoints, biomarkers, laboratory standardization, immunogenicity, safety, statistics, and regulatory strategy. The framework is applied to genome editing, RNA therapeutics, rebalancing agents, and synthetic coagulation proteins, drawing on published evidence through mid-2026 and the author's experience as a clinical trial investigator.Expert opinionTherapeutic success requires both molecular innovation and rigorous early-phase trial design. An ingenious product cannot compensate for failure to define its therapeutic window, clinically meaningful benefit, or implementation requirements. Experience with non-factor and gene therapies shows that mechanisms with compelling preclinical rationale may fail, cause harm, or remain clinically underused when durability, immunogenicity, and real-world implementation are treated as late-stage considerations. Addressing these issues from first-in-human studies will determine which emerging genome-editing and RNA-based candidates succeed.
records.authors: Mahlangu JN.

records.title: Heterologous expression of the Metarhizium anisopliae barc gene cluster reveals a diphenyl ether-to-xanthene transformation in barceloneic acid biosynthesis.
records.abstract: Filamentous fungi generate chemical diversity through several evolutionary strategies, including the elaboration of conserved biosynthetic intermediates into structurally distinct secondary metabolites. Emodin and its corresponding anthrone are central intermediates in fungal aromatic polyketide metabolism, yet the enzymatic logic that remodels these precursors into more complex scaffolds remains incompletely understood. To investigate this process, we examined an infection-responsive non-reducing polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster (barc) from the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae predicted to encode an emodin-derived aromatic polyketide pathway. Heterologous reconstruction of the barc cluster in Aspergillus nidulans led to the production of the previously reported diphenyl ether barceloneic acid A (1) and the xanthene barceloneic acid C2 (2), together with two new compounds derived from 2, barceloneic acids D and E (3 and 4). Compound 3 is a cyclopentanone adduct of the xanthene 2, whereas 4 is a polyketide-indole hybrid, highlighting the chemical reactivity of the xanthene 2 scaffold. Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2. This defines a previously uncharacterised oxidative scaffold-remodelling step in barceloneic acid biosynthesis, revealing how an emodin-derived pathway can access a xanthene scaffold. Deletion of the backbone gene barcB in M. anisopliae did not significantly alter virulence towards Tenebrio molitor (mealworm) under the conditions tested, suggesting that barceloneic acids are not essential for pathogenicity in this insect model.
records.authors: Sbaraini N, Bracegirdle J, Phan CS, Bulcock BW, Geremia F, da Silva Camargo M, Flematti GR, Lacey E, Staats CC, Piggott AM, Chooi YH.

records.title: Multi-month fouling control on UV-emitting glass: performance, energy dependence, and insights into microbial community drivers.
records.abstract: UV-emitting glass (UEG) offers a promising solution to control biofouling on submerged surfaces without the need for chemicals, yet its long-term efficacy under real marine conditions has not been established. In this study, UEG lenses designed for multi-month marine submersion were deployed for three months at Port Canaveral, FL, driven by 265 nm UV-LEDs at a 30 min on/off duty cycle to emit ∼55 μW/cm2 when submerged. The results showed that UEG surfaces maintain fouling coverage below 15% throughout the entire 12-week deployment, while controls reached 100% surface coverage within two weeks, a disparity that persisted and widened over the full deployment period. Control biofilm volume and thickness increased nearly four-fold between months one and three, producing dense barnacle- and bryozoan-dominated assemblages, whereas UEG surfaces remained near baseline. Microbially, controls followed canonical marine successional trajectories toward Pseudoalteromonas dominance while UEG treatment disrupted this progression and sustained significantly greater community evenness across both bacterial and eukaryotic domains. At current settings, the system consumed 127 Wh/day, with energy modeling suggesting meaningful reductions are achievable through irradiance and duty-cycle optimization.
records.authors: Alidokht L, Chavarria KA, Eggers D, Hunsucker K, Lanzarini-Lopes M.

records.title: Exploratory single-cell multiomics suggests naive CD4<sup>+</sup> T cell dysregulation in treatment refractory rheumatoid arthritis.
records.abstract: Around 20% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have disease that remains refractory to multiple targeted treatments, highlighting a major clinical challenge. We determine single-nucleus transcriptional and chromatin landscapes (10x Genomics Epi Multiome) on 14,625 primary CD4+ T-cells isolated from treatment-naive early and refractory (defined as per the EULAR definition of difficult-to-treat) patients with RA. We systematically analyze circulating regulatory profiles to reveal potential mechanisms and therapeutic targets that may contribute to the difficult-to-treat phenotype. We highlight disease-stage-specific alterations in naive and Th1-like memory CD4+ T-cells. In particular, refractory naive cells show signatures of heightened activation, upregulation of pathways aligning with T cell anergy, diminished regulation at regulatory loci (e.g., FOXP1, ICOS) and blunted stimulation responses; consistent with a more desensitized or exhausted state. Genes such as LGALS3, ZBTB7B and FOXO4 emerge as potential candidate regulators of the difficult-to-treat state. Finally, through RA GWAS integration, we prioritize putative causal variants in cis-regulatory elements.

records.title: Identification of potential regulators of caffeine biosynthesis in shading- and nano‑selenium-treated tea leaves based on integrated bioinformatics and AlphaFold3 analysis.
records.abstract: Caffeine is an important flavor and bioactive compound in tea, yet external stimuli-induced regulatory networks of caffeine biosynthesis remain largely unclear. Our study showed that shading and nano‑selenium (SeNPs) treatments respectively increased caffeine content in tea leaves from 35.96 mg/g to approximately 43 mg/g, whereas their combined treatment exerted a synergistic effect, raising it to 51.12 mg/g. Correlation of transcriptome with caffeine content and treatment factors via WGCNA and Mantel tests identified 4 key gene modules and 64 transcription factors (TFs). To accelerate TF screening, we established a rapid and high-throughput screening strategy by integrating AlphaFold3 with JASPAR motif prediction, resulting in 10 candidate TF-DNA complexes. Subsequent validation in yeast and tobacco systems confirmed that CsTSO1 directly binds to the promoter of CsSAMS. Our study uncovers how shading and SeNPs modulate caffeine biosynthesis in tea plants, and provide an AI-assisted framework for efficient TF screening in plant metabolic network.
records.authors: Ye J, Han Q, Zhu J, Li C.

records.title: Temporal Ecology of the Grapevine Microbiome: A Framework for Assembly, Persistence and Disease in Perennial Crops
records.abstract: Plant microbiome studies increasingly resolve community composition, but evidence derived largely from annual-plant models and cross-sectional surveys remains poorly suited to reconstruct ecological history in woody crops. We propose grapevine as an information-rich reference system for temporal microbiome ecology because clonal propagation, grafting, nursery-to-vineyard transfer, organs with contrasting lifespans, recurrent management and chronic disease align assembly processes across nested timescales. We synthesise current evidence into a four-clock framework spanning microbial arrival and establishment over days to weeks, seasonal organ renewal, multi-year field transitions and decades of host ageing and disease development. Grapevine compartments can be treated as a candidate connected metacommunity in which source pools, dispersal, abiotic and host filtering, and priority effects shape residence. Disturbance may elicit resistant, resilient or history-dependent responses. This framework separates pathogen detection from microbial activity, tissue damage and symptom expression, and views chronic disease as a trajectory in host-microbiome function. We identify the limits of current amplicon-based and cross-sectional evidence and propose designs combining individual-level longitudinal sampling, quantitative load, spatial and functional multi-omics, cultivation, synthetic communities and multisite validation. The framework generates testable hypotheses for separating temporal association from persistence, legacy, memory and disease causation across perennial crop systems.
records.authors: Eichmeier A, Li Y, Gramaje D.

records.title: Stress-response regulators tune enterobacterial common antigen synthesis to support acid and reactive nitrogen species stress resistance
records.abstract: Enteric bacteria must survive envelope-damaging environmental conditions in both host and environmental niches (e.g., acidic environments, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species). The Gram-negative outer membrane (OM) is central to the cell’s stress resistance, acting as a permeability barrier to antimicrobials and as an adaptable structure remodeled in response to environmental changes.  Enterobacterales (  e.g., Escherichia coli ,  Salmonella enterica ,  Klebsiella pneumoniae ) produce an invariant glycan, enterobacterial common antigen (ECA), which is localized in the OM and periplasm and contributes to the OM permeability barrier. Yet, how ECA biosynthesis is controlled and the conditions under which ECA is important remain poorly defined. Therefore, we investigated transcriptional regulation of the ECA biosynthesis  wec operon in  E. coli K-12. We assayed  wec operon promoter activity across deletions of 36 bioinformatically identified potential regulator genes and identified four for which deletion significantly altered  wec promoter activity. Of these, two repressors, GadX, a regulator of the glutamate-dependent acid stress response system, and MetJ, the master regulator of methionine biosynthesis and a reactive nitrogen species (RNS) stress regulator, bound to the  wec promoter  in vitro , consistent with direct transcriptional regulation. In accordance with a link between ECA and these regulators,  wec promoter activity increased under acidic pH and under RNS stress, and loss of ECA impaired growth under both conditions and fitness in acidic pH. Together, these findings reveal that biosynthesis of a conserved OM glycan is embedded within dedicated environmental stress regulons and identify previously unrecognized roles for ECA in bacterial stress adaptation.  Importance  Enteric bacteria rely on their cell envelope to survive chemical and physical stresses in changing environments. Enterobacterial common antigen (ECA), an invariant envelope glycan produced by enteric bacteria (  Enterobacterales ), plays a role in the outer membrane (OM) permeability barrier that excludes detergents and antibiotics. Despite its conservation, the cellular function of ECA, and the conditions that require it, remain elusive. Here, we define the transcriptional regulation of ECA biosynthesis and use it to identify environmental conditions in which ECA function is important for cellular growth. We identified regulators of two stress responses (GadX, an acid stress regulator, and MetJ, a reactive nitrogen species stress regulator) as direct repressors of ECA biosynthesis and show ECA promotes growth under both acid stress and reactive nitrogen species stress. These results indicate that a conserved envelope glycan is integrated into stress-response networks and functions broadly in adaptation to environmental stress.
records.authors: Hill HC, Mitchell AM.

records.title: Dual phage sensing activates an RNA-targeting reverse transcriptase for anti-phage defense
records.abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) mediate diverse antiphage responses, yet how they sense phage infection and couple unconventional DNA synthesis to antiviral effector activation remains poorly understood. Here, we characterize DRT4 as a dual-sensor immune system that integrates two distinct phage-derived signals. Cryo-EM analysis reveals that DRT4 assembles into a dimer-of-trimers hexamer, with each protomer catalyzing protein-primed, template-independent synthesis of a covalently linked ssDNA product. DRT4 displays a strong preference for purine nucleotides, determined by base-specific interactions within the polymerase active site. Using phage escape genetics, we identify two independent activators of DRT4: the phage ribonucleotide reductase NrdAB, which increase intracellular dNTP levels, and the SSB-like protein 0087, which directly binds the DRT4-generated ssDNA. Activated DRT4 exhibits dNTP-dependent RNase activity, linking phage sensing to RNA cleavage and abortive infection. Together, our findings show DRT4-generated ssDNA as a signaling intermediate that integrates phage-induced metabolic changes with direct recognition of viral replication proteins, revealing how protein-primed DNA synthesis can be repurposed for infection sensing and antiviral effector activation.
records.authors: Wei X, Qi H, Song X, Li L, Xia Y, Zhang J, Jia N.

records.title: Designing a reoriented H5 hemagglutinin to generate stem-directed, heterosubtypic immunity to influenza A viruses
records.abstract: Human infections with the highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses highlight the risk of novel pandemics, against which seasonal vaccines provide limited cross-protection. Whereas antibody responses to current vaccine candidates are typically biased toward the immunodominant and variable head region of hemagglutinin (HA), the stem region of HA is highly conserved and targeted by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Here we describe a reoriented H5 HA (reoH5HA  Phe , based on A/Vietnam/1203/2004) displayed on alum as a vaccine candidate to elicit stem-directed antibody responses and confer cross-protective immunity. We show that a single immunization with reoH5HA  Phe protected naïve mice against heterologous H5N1 lethal challenge (A/Texas/37/2024), and boosting with reoH5HA  Phe conferred complete heterologous protection in mice pre-immunized with seasonal vaccines. The stem-directed response elicited by reoH5HA  Phe also protected against heterosubtypic H1N1 challenge in both naïve and pre-immune mice. Electron microscopy polyclonal epitope mapping revealed that reoH5HA  Phe elicited antibodies targeting the central stem and anchor epitopes on heterologous H5 and H1 HAs, alongside antibodies against the (H5) vestigial esterase or (H1) lateral patch epitopes. Despite limited cross-neutralizing activity, increased stem-directed responses with balanced IgG1 and IgG2 subclasses reduced viral replication and improved survival. Our results highlight antigen reorientation as an effective approach for designing variant-resilient vaccines and demonstrate the potential of reoH5HA  Phe as an H5 pandemic influenza vaccine candidate that confers protective immunity against both emerging and seasonal influenza viruses.  Significance Statement  The global spread and human infections of avian H5N1 influenza viruses raise concerns of novel pandemics, against which humans lack pre-existing immunity. Whereas current vaccine strategies, including mRNA vaccines, mostly protect against sequence-matched viruses, pandemic preparedness requires vaccine design that resists antigenic variation and viral evolution. Here we employ molecular control of antigen orientation to focus antibody responses toward evolutionarily conserved sites of influenza hemagglutinin. We designed a reoriented H5 hemagglutinin based on the historical sequence (A/Vietnam/1203/2004) and demonstrated robust protection against the contemporary virus (A/Texas/37/2024). Vaccinations with reoriented H5 hemagglutinin also conferred protection against historical and contemporary H1N1 viruses. Our approach has potential to provide protection against emerging, pandemic-potential viruses, while simultaneously boosting immunity to seasonal influenza viruses.

records.title: Two conserved early effectors from Puccinia triticina are required for pathogenicity by suppressing callose deposition and hydrogen peroxide accumulation in wheat.
records.abstract: BackgroundWheat leaf rust, caused by the causal agent Puccinia triticina (Pt), poses a serious threat to wheat production worldwide. Pt secretes plenty of effectors into the host plant to manipulate host immune responses and facilitate successful colonization. However, effectors during the early stages of Pt infection remain largely unknown.ResultsHere, we employed deep RNA-sequencing on samples extracted from wheat leaves of a susceptible wheat cultivar, Thatcher, inoculated with Pt at 8 and 24 h post-inoculation, which enabled the identification of candidate effectors implicated in suppressing early plant immune responses. Through integrated transcriptomic analysis and an optimized effector identification workflow, early candidate effector-encoding genes that are highly expressed during Pt infection were identified and characterized. Functional assays revealed that two effector candidates, Pt01364 and Pt09156, exhibited the ability to suppress Bax-induced cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana. Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis demonstrated that both genes peaked at 8 h post-inoculation, and the yeast secretion trap assay showed that these two cell death-suppressing effector candidates possess functional signal peptides for secretion into host cells. Silencing of Pt01364 and Pt09156 significantly compromised Pt pathogenicity on a susceptible wheat cultivar. In addition, both effectors can inhibit callose deposition triggered by non-host bacteria and reduce hydrogen peroxide accumulation in wheat in response to avirulent Pt infection.ConclusionThis study provides a basis for identifying key effectors involved in the early stages of wheat-Pt interaction, highlighting Pt01364 and Pt09156 as promising candidate targets for developing innovative strategies to control wheat leaf rust. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

records.title: Efficacy of Heat-Killed Lactobacillus plantarum L-137 Supplementation in Treatment of Canine Atopic Dermatitis.
records.abstract: BackgroundCanine atopic dermatitis (cAD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease and has been associated with gut dysbiosis.Hypothesis/objectivesTo evaluate the efficacy of heat-killed Lactobacillus plantarum L-137 (HK L-137), a postbiotic supplementation in managing cAD.AnimalsTwelve client-owned dogs with cAD.Materials and methodsA randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blinded crossover trial. Dogs were divided into two groups (n = 6) and received oral HK L-137 or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. After a 2-week washout period, they received the alternative treatment. Oral oclacitinib (0.4-0.6 mg/kg once daily) was permitted throughout the study. Clinical severity was assessed with the 4th iteration of the cAD Extent and Severity Index (CADESI-04) and owner-evaluated pruritus Visual Analog Scale (PVAS) and faecal scoring at 0, 12, 14 and 26 weeks. Serum concentrations of C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin (IL)-4, interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and C-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CCL17), and haematological and biochemical findings were analysed at the same time points. Faecal microbiota composition (genomic DNA) was assessed at 12 and 26 weeks.ResultsPVAS scores mildly improved in both groups, with greater reduction in the HK L-137 group, yet this was not statistically significant. Serum CRP concentrations increased significantly in the control group (p = 0.02). Serum CCL17 concentrations decreased significantly in the HK L-137 group (p = 0.01). No significant changes were observed in CADESI-04, IL-4, IFN-γ or faecal scores or faecal microbiota diversity and composition.Conclusions and clinical relevanceHK L-137 represents a potential, well-tolerated adjunctive therapy for dogs with cAD. Therapy was associated with reduced CCL17. Further studies with fewer variables are indicated.
records.authors: Kiewsiri C, Patumcharoenpol P, Kovitvadhi A, Chermprapai S.

records.title: The JAK3/IL-2Rα axis in Helicobacter pylori-associated macrophage reprogramming: A narrative review of a proposed immunoregulatory framework.
records.abstract: This narrative review examines the role of macrophage reprogramming in Helicobacter pylori infection. H. pylori colonizes the human gastric mucosa and is a major risk factor for chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, and gastric cancer. Persistent infection depends on bacterial virulence factors and the bacterium's capacity to reshape host immunity. Macrophages play a central role in gastric mucosal defense by participating in bacterial recognition, phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and cytokine production. However, during chronic infection, macrophage effector functions may become progressively impaired, favoring bacterial persistence. The interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain (IL-2Rα, also termed CD25) and downstream Janus kinase 3 (JAK3)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5) signaling have been proposed to contribute to an immunoregulatory macrophage state, although direct evidence in the infected gastric mucosa remains limited. This review critically evaluates the available evidence for and against a role of the JAK3/IL-2Rα axis in H. pylori-associated macrophage reprogramming. We describe the structural and signaling basis of the IL-2 receptor complex, summarize the multifactorial regulation of macrophage phenotypes during infection, and examine the JAK3/IL-2Rα axis within a broader network that includes TNF/TNFR1-NLRP3, JAK1/2-STAT1, JAK3-SOCS3, autophagy, and metabolic pathways. We also discuss the therapeutic implications and major knowledge gaps. The available primary data, including findings from a previous study by some of the present authors, indicate a pro-inflammatory, M1-like acute response rather than a classical M2 state. Furthermore, macrophage-specific activation of a tolerogenic program in infected gastric tissue has not been directly demonstrated. Accordingly, the JAK3/IL-2Rα pathway is presented as a context-dependent hypothesis requiring further investigation rather than as an established mechanism.

records.title: Chronic Wounds as Biofilm Ecosystems: Modernizing Microbiology Beyond Planktonic Paradigms.
records.abstract: SignificanceChronic wound infections, including diabetic foot infections, are increasingly recognized as biofilm-associated polymicrobial ecosystems rather than simple planktonic infections. However, routine microbiological workflows remain largely optimized for acute infections, creating a mismatch between laboratory diagnostics and the biological organization of chronic infection.Recent advancesGrowing evidence from biofilm biology, microbial ecology, and molecular microbiology has demonstrated that chronic wound infections are characterized by structured microbial communities, physiological heterogeneity, and enhanced antimicrobial tolerance. Advanced diagnostic approaches have improved understanding of microbial diversity and biofilm-associated persistence beyond what is captured by conventional culture alone.Critical issuesConventional microbiological workflows may incompletely resolve the microbial populations most relevant to chronicity, recurrence, and treatment failure. Key limitations include sampling strategy, tissue processing, incubation conditions, anaerobic recovery, and reliance on planktonic susceptibility testing. The discrepancy between minimum inhibitory concentration-based testing and biofilm-associated antimicrobial tolerance highlights an important gap between laboratory assessment and infection biology.Future directionsModernization of chronic wound microbiology requires a transition from pathogen-centered planktonic models toward biofilm-aware, ecosystem-oriented approaches. Integration of optimized sampling, culture-based diagnostics, selective molecular tools, surgical source control, and antimicrobial stewardship may improve diagnostic resolution, support more rational antimicrobial use, and enhance long-term clinical outcomes.[Figure: see text].

records.title: Liquid crystalline nanoparticle-mediated co-delivery of gentamicin and rhDNase against mature Escherichia coli biofilms.
records.abstract: Biofilm-associated infections remain a major clinical challenge due to restricted antibiotic penetration, matrix-mediated antimicrobial tolerance, and rapid degradation of biofilm-disruptive therapeutics in protease-rich environments. Here, liquid crystalline nanoparticles (LCNPs) were developed as a nanostructured co-delivery platform for gentamicin (GEN) and recombinant human DNase I (rhDNase), integrating antibiotic delivery with enzymatic disruption of the biofilm extracellular matrix. LCNPs exhibited favourable physicochemical properties, including nanoscale particle size, low polydispersity, and preservation of cubosome-like internal morphology following enzyme incorporation. High encapsulation efficiencies were achieved for GEN (∼95%) and rhDNase (∼94%). Compared with conventional liposomes, LCNPs demonstrated sustained GEN release, prolonged rhDNase retention, and improved protection of rhDNase against proteolytic degradation, highlighting the role of the liquid crystalline matrix in therapeutic retention and enzyme stability. Antibiofilm studies against mature Escherichia coli biofilms showed concentration-dependent potentiation of GEN activity by rhDNase, with further enhancement through LCNP-mediated co-delivery. While unformulated GEN produced modest biofilm reduction (∼20-30%), optimised GEN + rhDNase-LCNPs reduced residual biofilm biomass to ∼25-30% of untreated controls and produced ∼5-6 log reductions in recoverable biofilm-associated bacteria in MBEC assays. Confocal imaging showed a broader distribution of membrane-compromised bacteria across the imaged biofilm field following LCNP-mediated co-delivery, without directly resolving penetration depth. LCNP formulations also maintained favourable cytocompatibility at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Overall, these findings provide proof-of-concept that LCNP-mediated co-delivery can improve GEN activity against mature E. coli ATCC 25922 biofilms while protecting rhDNase; validation across additional strains, clinical isolates, and bacterial species is required before broader antibiofilm generalisation.
records.authors: Ahsan A, Barnes TJ, Thomas N, Prestidge CA.

records.title: Exploration of the therapeutic mechanisms of nuciferine in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome treatment based on multi-omics approaches.
records.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is one of the most common reproductive endocrine and metabolic diseases affecting women's health. Here, we investigated the effect of nuciferine (NUC) on PMOS in vivo experiments. For transcriptome sequencing analysis and verification results, NUC mainly affected PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways in liver tissue and affected PI3K-AKT and NF-κB pathway in adipose tissue, respectively. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the binding of PI3K to NUC is more effective. Meanwhile.Indole-3-acetic acid and Tryptamine were the key production of intestinal flora regulated by NUC after integrating metagenomics and non-targeted metabolomics analysis. The study confirmed the efficacy of NUC in DHEA - induced PMOS mice. PI3K might be the key target protein and Indole-3-acetic acid and Tryptamine were the key production regulated by NUC in PMOS treatment.
records.authors: Li JT, Zhang SM, Jiang X, Liu DL, Wang ZG, Zhao HX.

records.title: Construction of multigene-deletion Vibrio parahaemolyticus strains and preliminary evaluation of their short-term protective effects in Litopenaeus vannamei.
records.abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus is an important pathogen in shrimp aquaculture. To assess multi-gene attenuation as a basis for live-vaccine development, we constructed Δhlyd-hlyIII and Δhlyd-hlyIII-ompn mutants and evaluated their phenotypes, transcriptomic profiles, attenuation, and short-term protective effects in Litopenaeus vannamei. Compared with the wild-type (WT) strain, the mutants showed reduced swimming motility, extracellular protease and hemolytic activities, and biofilm formation; biofilm biomass decreased by 73.94% and 83.55% in the double- and triple-deletion mutants, respectively. Exploratory RNA sequencing of pooled RNA samples identified 2391 genes that met the original differential-expression screening criteria in the triple-deletion mutant relative to WT (1073 upregulated and 1318 downregulated; adjusted P ≤ 0.05 and |log₂ fold change| ≥ 1). ABC transporters and flagellar assembly were significantly enriched among the downregulated genes after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (adjusted P 6-1.00 × 109 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL, mortality was 32-66% for WT and 16-40% for the triple-deletion mutant. The corresponding 7-day immersion median lethal dose (LD50) estimates were 2.86 × 107 and >1.00 × 109 CFU/mL, respectively. Survival was also monitored during primary and booster immersion on days 0 and 7, before WT challenge on day 12. In the experiment, which used one tank per treatment group, both mutant-exposed groups had lower survival before challenge than the PBS-treated control but higher survival after WT challenge than the unimmunized challenged-control group. These findings support further evaluation of Δhlyd-hlyIII-ompn as a live attenuated immersion vaccine candidate against V. parahaemolyticus in L. vannamei.

records.title: Molecular epidemiological investigation of bovine coronavirus in some areas of Inner Mongolia and genetic evolution analysis of the S gene.
records.abstract: BackgroundBovine coronavirus (BCoV) is a significant pathogen responsible for neonatal calf diarrhea and respiratory disorders. The spike (S) protein plays a pivotal role in mediating viral entry into host cells and eliciting immune responses. This study conducted a comprehensive analysis of the complete S gene sequences from field isolates.ResultsNested PCR screening of 236 fecal samples collected from nine leagues and cities in Inner Mongolia yielded a positive rate of 7.63% (18/236), with marked regional variation; notably, Hinggan (Xing'an) League accounted for the largest proportion of positive cases (38.89%, 7/18 of total positives). Four complete S gene sequences (4092 bp) were obtained from positive specimens. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the Inner Mongolian strains clustered within the Genogroup II (GII) lineage. Comparative analysis of the S protein amino acid sequences identified seven variation sites. Bioinformatics prediction suggested that the variant strain may possess altered antigenic properties, although these computational predictions require experimental validation. While the transmembrane domain (1308-1328) and the signal peptide cleavage site were highly conserved, variations in glycosylation and phosphorylation sites were observed. The secondary structure was predominantly composed of random coils (51.65% - 52.24%), suggesting structural flexibility. Furthermore, key functional motifs were conserved, although mutations within the receptor-binding domain (RBD), such as G573E, were identified, which warrant further investigation to determine their functional implications.ConclusionsThis study provides a preliminary investigation into the epidemiology of BCoV in Inner Mongolia and analyzes the genetic variation of the S protein. These findings offer descriptive insights into the epidemiological patterns of BCoV in Inner Mongolia and establish a baseline for continuous molecular surveillance. While the identified genetic variations may provide reference information for future research, including vaccine-related studies, such implications remain speculative and would require extensive experimental validation.

records.title: TFXcan reveals transcription factor programs driving GWAS loci.
records.abstract: Disease-associated loci identified by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) may induce effects by altering transcription factor (TF) binding. However, due to the scarcity of population-level TF-binding experiments, identifying these disrupted TFs remains challenging. To address this, we present the TFXcan framework, which correlates genetically predicted TF binding with phenotypes to nominate TF-tissue pairs that may regulate complex traits. Within this framework, we introduce Enpact, a deep learning-based approach that integrates Enformer and IMPACT to infer personalized TF-binding events. Leveraging Enpact, we correlate predicted binding profiles for 700 TF-tissue pairs with prostate cancer risk, identifying multiple implicated TFs at risk loci. Matrix decomposition further reveals clusters of TF-tissue pairs, termed "programs," acting as candidate drivers of disease risk. TFXcan represents the first method capable of predicting TF binding from genotype data at scale, enabling systematic identification of TFs and regulatory programs underlying complex traits.

records.title: A voltage-gated porin PPE1 regulates secretion and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
records.abstract: Drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a formidable clinical hurdle, compounded by the fact that the pathways by which antibiotics penetrate its multilayered cell envelope remain incompletely mapped. We identify PPE1 as a voltage-gated outer-membrane porin that mediates the secretion of kupyaphores while also facilitating the uptake of the frontline anti-tubercular drug isoniazid (INH). Genome-wide association analysis of 38,038 clinical isolates links ppe1 mutations with INH resistance, highlighting its clinical relevance. Consistent with this, the Mtb Δppe1 mutant shows increased tolerance to INH, accompanied by markedly reduced intracellular accumulation of INH compared with the wild-type strain. The Δppe1 strain exhibits attenuated infection, impaired growth, and reduced virulence in a murine infection model. Electron microscopy, molecular modeling, and single-channel electrophysiology reveal that PPE1 assembles into an unusual pentameric α-helical channel, distinct from classical β-barrel bacterial porins. Together, our findings identify PPE1 as a key determinant of mycobacterial membrane permeability that coordinates metallophore secretion and also antibiotic influx. This work uncovers a previously unrecognized mechanism governing Mtb physiology, virulence, and drug susceptibility, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

records.title: Transcriptomic Profiling of PBMCs via Bulk RNA-Sequencing in Posner-Schlossman Syndrome Reveals Immune Dysregulation and Altered Viral Response.
records.abstract: PurposeTo explore systemic immune transcriptional signatures in Posner-Schlossman syndrome (PSS) across acute and intermittent phases.MethodsBulk RNA sequencing was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from acute-phase PSS patients (APSS; n = 4), intermittent-phase PSS patients (IPSS; n = 3), and healthy controls (n = 3). Two patients were sampled in both phases; within-subject correlation was not modeled in differential-expression analyses. Differential expression was assessed using DESeq2, pathways were examined using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, and immune-cell-associated marker expression was compared using CAMERA gene set testing with linear model contrasts. Plasma IFITM2, ISG15, and SOCS1 were measured by ELISA in an independent cohort of 51 APSS patients and 69 healthy controls.ResultsInterferon-responsive and antiviral genes, including IFITM2, ISG15, and SOCS1, were downregulated in APSS. Plasma protein levels showed concordant decreases in the independent cohort. Genes encoding ubiquitin-proteasome components (SKP1, RBX1, PSMF1, PSMB2, PSMB3, and PSMD13) and cytokines associated with antigen presentation and adaptive immunity were downregulated, whereas cytokine genes linked to macrophage activity and innate immunity were upregulated. Post hoc comparisons showed reduced CD8+ T-cell-associated and increased macrophage-associated marker expression in APSS compared with both IPSS and controls. IPSS immune transcriptional profiles generally approached those of controls, consistent with reduced disease activity, although residual differences in macrophage-associated expression remained.ConclusionsThese exploratory findings suggest altered systemic innate and adaptive immune regulation in PSS, with an increased monocyte/macrophage-associated transcriptional signature during acute attacks. They do not establish immune-cell proportions or cytomegalovirus-mediated mechanisms and cannot directly represent local anterior chamber pathology.
records.authors: Peng SM, Zhu TH, He J, Huang XS, Ye Y, Deng HW.

records.title: Genome-wide association study identifies genomic regions associated with milk composition and fatty acid traits in Indian Holstein Friesian crossbred cattle.
records.abstract: BackgroundCrossbred cattle play a pivotal role in India's milk production. This study aimed to identify genomic regions and candidate genes associated with milk yield, milk composition, fatty acid (FA) profile, and desaturase indices in Holstein Friesian crossbred cattle (HFCB).Methods and resultsA total of 128 HFCB animals were genotyped using 53,218 SNPs, of which 44,128 passed quality control for Genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis. Phenotypic evaluation showed moderate variation in test-day milk yield (TDMY) and milk composition traits, while FA profiling revealed predominance of long-chain FAs, particularly palmitic and oleic acids. GWAS identified 36 SNPs across multiple chromosomes, one statistically significant and 35 suggestive. A pleiotropic SNP (ARS-BFGL-NGS-96359) on the Bos Taurus autosome (BTA) 24 was associated with lactose, protein, and solids-not-fat percentages. Several SNPs were associated with short-, medium-, and long-chain saturated fatty acids, with positive and negative allelic effects. Notable effect sizes were observed for oleic acid (C18:1cis) and desaturase indices, particularly DI C17. Positional candidate gene analysis identified HACL1, SGPP2, IMMP2L, MYO5B, ZNF536, GADD45A, PRDM9, and PROKR2, which are involved in lipid metabolism and cellular regulation. Individual SNPs explained 0.087-0.194 of the phenotypic variance, with several loci contributing substantially to milk composition traits and FA C4, C10, and C15.ConclusionsThis study highlights the polygenic nature of milk production and quality traits in HFCB cattle. The study also provides preliminary insights into the genetic architecture of milk quality traits and may contribute to future genomic selection efforts following validation in larger and independent populations.
records.authors: Yadav A, Singh R, Khan KD, Alex R, Gowane GR.

records.title: Hierarchically Gated DNA Nanoswitches Enable Context-Selective Activation of Antimicrobial Peptides.
records.abstract: Precise control over cytolytic peptide activity remains a central challenge in antimicrobial therapy because membrane disruption is intrinsically coupled with systemic toxicity. Here we encode a hierarchically gated molecular logic within a DNA nanoswitch to enable context-selective activation of melittin only at infection sites. The nanoswitch integrates three cooperative control layers: bacterial tropism, microenvironmental sensing, and inflammation-associated enzymatic activation. Maltodextrin ligands are spatially programmed to engage the bacteria-specific maltodextrin transporter, yielding selective bacterial recognition with a 2.3-order-of-magnitude enhancement in binding. Cytosine-rich i-motif locks convert acidic biofilm conditions into conformational opening of the scaffold, while a caspase-1-cleavable peptide tether provides a final enzymatic gate under inflammatory cues. This hierarchical gating confines membrane-lytic activity with high spatiotemporal precision and suppresses off-target hemolysis and systemic leakage. In uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC)-associated urinary tract infection models, the nanoswitch achieves effective bacterial clearance comparable to that of ciprofloxacin in vivo, demonstrating a generalizable strategy for conditional peptide activation.

records.title: Comparing the Phenotypic and Genetic Differences Between Autistic Regression and Autism Without Regression Using the SPARK Cohort
records.abstract: The biology of autistic regression (Autreg) remains poorly understood. We investigated Autreg’s phenotypic and genetic landscape in 51 633 individuals from the SPARK cohort. We calculated the frequencies of parental-reported language regression and regression affecting social, play, toileting, and/or other developmental domains, and ages at skill regression and regain within SPARK. We compared developmental milestones, quantitative developmental measures, and selected other phenotypes in Autreg and autism without regression (Autnreg). Rare damaging coding variants and polygenic scores (PGS) in Autreg and Autnreg were compared using genome sequencing data. Rare variants were analyzed using the Transmission And De novo Association (TADA) framework in 1 107 Autreg and 974 Autnreg individuals, followed by pathway enrichment analysis. PGS for autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, epilepsy, and schizophrenia were initially compared. PGS validation was conducted in 14 001 Autnreg and 11 638 Autreg individuals using larger SPARK genotyping data. We identified regression in 43% of autistic individuals. Other regression occurred later than language regression, and 60% of skill regain occurred within two years. Autreg was associated with lower Vineland-3 Adaptive Behavior Composite scores (ptwofold increased odds of epilepsy and intellectual disability (p<0.001). Developmental milestones and quantitative measures had modest differences. TADA analysis highlighted genes involved in nucleotide catabolism, transcription, and focal adhesion, with  PTEN emerging as a strong candidate for Autreg. Schizophrenia PGS explained 0.087% of variance in liability to regression among autistic individuals. In conclusion, Autreg was associated with increased neurodevelopmental morbidity. Schizophrenia PGS and rare variants explained a minimal fraction of its etiology.
records.authors: Yahia A, Zhang Y, Gkerdi A, Rajagopalan SS, Tammimies K.

records.title: Isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight but not relative adiposity, adipose inflammation, or gut microbial diversity in high-fat diet-fed mice
records.abstract: Background/Objectives  The separate contributions of excess energy intake and diet composition to high-fat diet (HFD)-induced adiposity, adipose inflammation, and gut microbial changes are unclear. We tested whether restricting HFD intake to the energy intake of low-fat (LF)-fed mice (isocaloric restriction) prevents or reverses these outcomes. Subjects/Methods  Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8/group) received for 12 weeks an LF diet (LF/LF) or HFD (HF/HF) ad libitum, HFD ad libitum then isocaloric HFD from week 7 (HF/IHF), or isocaloric HFD throughout (IHF/IHF). Adiposity, plasma markers, adipose and ileal gene expression, and fecal microbiota (16S rRNA sequencing, n = 4/group) were assessed. Results  Final body weight in IHF/IHF did not differ from LF/LF (difference 0.1 g, 95% CI −6.5 to 6.7;  P > 0.99) and was lower than in HF/HF (−8.2 g, −14.7 to −1.6;  P = 0.011). Switching to isocaloric feeding reduced weight gain during weeks 6–12 (HF/IHF vs HF/HF, −6.4 g, −9.8 to −3.1;  P Conclusions  Limiting HFD energy intake normalized body weight, glycemia, and plasma lipids but not relative adiposity, adipose  Tnf expression, or the loss of gut microbial diversity. Diet composition affects these outcomes independently of energy intake, so normal body weight does not indicate their reversal.

records.title: Inferring somatic copy number aberrations from spatial transcriptomics data to study early cancer development
records.abstract: Understanding the spatial organisation of cells undergoing early transformation and their interactions with the local microenvironment is critical to studying the earliest stages of cancer development. Somatic copy number aberrations (SCNAs) are among the earliest genomic alterations observed in many cancers, but their spatial context remains difficult to study using conventional sequencing approaches. We developed a computational framework to infer SCNAs directly from Xenium spatial transcriptomics data, enabling the identification and spatial mapping of cell populations sharing common SCNA profiles. Applying this approach to ovarian, cervical and breast cancer datasets identified spatially coherent SCNA-defined populations that recapitulated known tumour-associated copy number aberrations and pathological states. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, we identified an intermediate epithelial population within the fallopian tube exhibiting features of early transformation accompanied by immune remodelling. Together, our pipeline establishes a scalable framework for reconstructing the spatial architecture of SCNA-defined clones, providing new opportunities to identify and characterise candidate early transforming cell populations in situ.
records.authors: Honig F, Brochen C, Basha M, Arora R, Jimenez-Linan M, Antoniou A, Rueda OM, Correia Martins F.

records.title: Vascular Steatosis as a Proposed Mechanism of Metabolic Hypertension: From Arterial Lipid Accumulation to Increased Vascular Resistance
records.abstract: Abstract    Introduction:  Hypertension remains the leading modifiable determinant of cardiovascular morbidity worldwide. Metabolic disease frequently coexists with elevated pressure, yet no vessel-level lesion has been clearly defined that converts systemic lipid excess into sustained vascular resistance.  Objective:  We propose vascular steatosis, defined as lipid accumulation within the arterial wall, as a candidate mechanism of metabolic hypertension and test its molecular and genetic support using human arterial transcriptomes and Mendelian randomization.  Methods:  This in silico study used two public arterial transcriptomes (GSE100927 for discovery, GSE43292 for paired validation). Summary-level Mendelian randomization used GTEx v8 cis-eQTLs from aorta, coronary, and tibial arteries, with whole blood as negative control, and blood pressure statistics from a European-ancestry genome-wide association study. Sensitivity and colocalization analyses followed.  Results:  Lesioned arteries showed upregulated CD36, ABCA1, and PLIN2, and downregulation of ACTA2, MYH11, and CNN1. Lipid-handling and contractile module scores were inversely associated (β = -0.42; 95% CI, -0.56 to -0.28), including in control arteries (β = -0.38), and the direction replicated in the validation set (β = -0.35). Genetically higher PLIN2 expression in aorta and CD36 expression in coronary artery were associated with higher blood pressure traits (FDR Conclusion:  Arterial lipid-handling programs track with loss of the contractile smooth muscle phenotype, and genetically proxied PLIN2 and CD36 expression is associated with blood pressure, which offers a biologically plausible and testable framework for the mechanistic classification of metabolic hypertension. Lipid quantification and physiological validation in resistance arteries are required to establish causal and clinical relevance.

records.abstract: Abstract    Early detection of transplant rejection remains a major unmet clinical need because histopathology is invasive, episodic, and subject to sampling error, whereas serum creatinine and other routine chemistries often rise only after injury is established [1–4]. records.title: AdhE Regulates the Adaptation Ability of Streptococcus mutans to Oxidative Stress and Heat Stress.
records.abstract: Understanding how S. mutans adapts to environmental stresses is key to deciphering its cariogenic virulence. Here, we report that alcohol-acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (AdhE) modulates the stress adaptability in S. mutans by regulating a metabolic-acetylation axis. We demonstrated that overexpression of adhE sensitizes S. mutans to H2O2 and high temperature, impairing planktonic growth and biofilm integrity under oxidative and heat stress. Mechanistically, AdhE functions as a potential acetyl-CoA (Ac-CoA) synthase, with its overexpression elevating intracellular Ac-CoA levels. Quantitative acetylomics revealed that elevated Ac-CoA drives extensive protein acetylation, hyperacetylating 340 proteins. Protein interaction network analysis identified core antioxidant enzymes (Tpx, Dpr, TrxA/B, AhpC) and heat-shock chaperones (DnaJ, GroEL, ClpE) as major targets, linking hyperacetylation to compromised stress defenses. Crucially, in a rat caries model, adhE overexpression attenuated the cariogenic virulence of S. mutans, reducing oral colonization and caries severity, an effect exacerbated by H2O2 challenge. Collectively, these findings uncover AdhE as a metabolic regulator that bridges Ac-CoA availability, global protein acetylation, and stress adaptation, offering new insights into posttranslational control of bacterial fitness and potential anti‑caries targets.
records.authors: Lin Y, Ma Q, Zhou X, Gong T, Lei Z, Wang S, Li Y.

records.title: Sucrose Reshapes the Extracellular Protein-Peptide Landscape of Streptococcus mutans and Identifies Peptide Candidates With Antibiofilm Activity.
records.abstract: The extracellular molecular landscape of oral bacteria remains underexplored beyond canonical secreted proteins. Here, we show that sucrose reshapes the culture-supernatant protein-peptide output of the cariogenic pathobiont Streptococcus mutans UA159. Integrating proteomics with stringent peptidomic source assignment revealed that sucrose remodeled the supernatant-detectable proteome toward surface/envelope- and cell-wall-associated features while reducing cytoplasmic, metabolic, and glucosyltransferase-associated signatures. In parallel, sucrose was associated with a distinct endogenous peptide layer. Among 34 stringently defined UA159-derived peptide candidates, 19 mapped to signal peptide regions, and many were preferentially detected under the sucrose condition. Functional screening of 16 successfully synthesized candidates identified two BHIS-associated signal-peptide-region peptides, SmuG15 and SmuV13, that reduced biofilm biomass and glucan-associated matrix signals when supplied exogenously, without detectable inhibition of planktonic growth in brain heart infusion (BHI). This separation between planktonic-growth and biofilm phenotypes is consistent with a biofilm-associated effect rather than detectable bacteriostatic activity under the planktonic-growth conditions tested. Together, these findings identify culture-supernatant peptides as sucrose-responsive extracellular outputs and highlight peptide candidates whose synthetic counterparts showed antibiofilm activity upon exogenous application. The study expands the molecular view of sucrose-driven cariogenic adaptation and provides a framework for discovering functional peptides from bacterial extracellular compartments.

records.title: Global diversification and regional spread of Candidozyma (Candida) auris clades: a comparative genomic epidemiology review of the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific.
records.abstract: Candidozyma auris (formerly Candida auris), first described in 2009, has spread to 82 countries across 6 continents, with more than 84,000 cumulative colonization and infection cases reported through December 2025. Whole-genome sequencing has resolved the species into six deeply divergent clades (I-VI) that differ geographically and in antifungal susceptibility. This minireview synthesizes peer-reviewed literature and public health surveillance data on whole-genome-sequencing-confirmed clade distribution and susceptibility across the United States, the European Union/European Economic Area, the United Kingdom, Latin America and the Caribbean, Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf region, Canada, Singapore, Australia, and New Zealand. Clades I and III are now the most geographically widespread outbreak-associated lineages, documented across nearly every region reviewed. The United States has diversified from early clade I dominance to a four-clade landscape by 2013-2022 (clade I, 56.0%; clade III, 29.4%; clade IV, 14.1%; and clade II, 0.5%). Latin America remains the principal reservoir of clade IV; Saudi Arabia and the Gulf region are dominated by clade I, and the discovery of clade VI in Singapore and Bangladesh illustrates continuing genomic diversification. Clade I carries the highest burden of multidrug and pan-resistance; clade III shows high fluconazole resistance but lower echinocandin resistance; and clade IV, historically associated with lower resistance, is now rising. Because regional antifungal resistance largely reflects clade composition rather than independent regional drift, clade-aware surveillance should directly inform local stewardship, diagnostic inclusivity, and regulatory bridging across markets.

records.title: Valid and included novel bacterial taxa isolated from aquatic host species described in 2024-2025.
records.abstract: The description of new taxa and nomenclature updates to currently known taxa from aquatic animal species continues at a rapid pace. After a review of the literature from 2024 to 2025, bacteria in major morphologic categories were compiled. As previously noted, bacteria characterized as oxidase-positive Gram-negative bacilli predominated. Additions included new taxa in common families associated with aquatic environments like Aeromonadaceae, Flavobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonadaceae, as well as more uncommon families, such as Pasteurellaceae. A number of Gram-positive organisms are noted, including Planococcus notacanthi sp. nov., the sole coccus described, and multiple bacilli, including new taxa in the Streptomyces and Paenibacillus genera. Two anaerobic species are highlighted, as well as a spirochete and a new member of family Chlamydiaceae. Revised taxa are briefly mentioned. As in previous reviews, most new and revised taxa are isolated from healthy aquatic animals, and the role of these new bacteria in health and disease has yet to be elucidated. Bacteria with potential clinical significance for aquatic animals or potential production of bioactive or antimicrobial substances are highlighted.
records.authors: de Ruyter TE, Burbick CR, Lawhon SD, Krueger T, Javier L, Munson E.

records.title: Modeling the Epstein-Barr virus lifecycle in the rabbit.
records.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a human gammaherpesvirus that establishes a lifelong, persistent infection in greater than 90% of people worldwide. EBV has lacked an animal model that depicts the viral lifecycle in B cells and epithelial cells, allows for the investigation of immune responses, and models persistence in a host. EBV establishes a robust infection in immunosuppressed rabbits, resulting in widespread infection of the spleen and the development of splenomegaly. Within the spleen, follicle formation was altered as a result of EBV infection. Similar magnitudes of infection were observed in immunosuppressed rabbits infected with the B95-8 and Akata viral strains. In immunocompetent rabbits, spleen morphology appeared similar to that of mock-infected rabbits. Rabbits infected with B95-8 and Akata viruses developed antibody responses to the EBNA family of proteins in a comparable manner to human infection. Akata infections were more consistent in both the immunosuppressed and immunocompetent studies, whereas B95-8 infections resulted in variable magnitudes of infection and immune responses. The persistence of EBV in rabbits and whether the full lifecycle of EBV in lymphocytes can be replicated remain to be further examined.ImportanceThe human gammaherpesvirus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 90% of the global population and is associated with lymphomas and carcinomas. EBV develops a lifelong, persistent infection in its host, avoiding immune detection by limiting the expression of its productive and latency genes. Currently, the EBV field lacks an animal model that can have persistent infection and immune responses to the virus during the course of infection. We demonstrated that rabbits mount an immune response to EBV infection over 6 months and may be a good model of persistent infection, although the viral genome remained below our limit of detection similar to humans.

records.title: Acetate scavenging and aromatic funneling of lignocellulose-derived carbon in the denitrifier Pseudomonas veronii.
records.abstract: Lignocellulose degradation and denitrification frequently co-occur in soils and sediments with fluctuating or limited O2 availability, yet the ability of facultative denitrifiers to couple aromatic carbon turnover to nitrate respiration remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized a novel isolate, Pseudomonas veronii strain B19, for its genetic potential and physiological performance during growth on hemicellulose- and lignin-derived substrates under oxic and denitrifying conditions. Genome analysis revealed extensive aromatic catabolic pathways, including a complete β-ketoadipate route funneling lignin-derived compounds to central metabolism. Despite lacking classical endo-xylanases, the strain grew on acetylated xylan, with faster denitrification kinetics than on glucose. Proteomic and electron flow analyses indicate that xylan utilization proceeds via deacetylation and acetate assimilation through acetyl-CoA. Notably, the carbon source governed the denitrification regulatory phenotype: glucose elicited bet hedging and transient nitrite accumulation at the oxic-anoxic transition, whereas xylan-derived acetate supported a seamless transition to denitrification. On alkali-solubilized lignin, the strain utilized soluble monoaromatic compounds under both oxic and denitrifying conditions. Oxic metabolism proceeded through strong induction of O2-dependent mono- and dioxygenases, enabling extensive aromatic catabolism, whereas under denitrifying conditions, conversion was only partial, with vanillate accumulation and electron-limited but stoichiometrically efficient nitrate reduction at minimal N2O formation. Together, these findings demonstrate that B19 links lignocellulose-derived carbon turnover to denitrification under limited O2, prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Its preference for soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin fractions and converging catabolic pathways indicate a role in downstream turnover of already-depolymerized lignin-derived aromatics, consistent with biological funneling and relevant to lignin valorization.IMPORTANCEDenitrification and the breakdown of plant-derived carbon are central to nitrogen and carbon cycling in soils and sediments, yet how these processes intersect when oxygen is scarce is poorly understood. Most denitrifiers are thought to rely on simple carbon sources, while the breakdown of polymeric lignin is considered oxygen-dependent. Here, we show that the facultative anaerobe Pseudomonas veronii B19 couples the turnover of acetylated hemicellulose and soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin-derived aromatics to denitrification, sustaining respiration under oxygen limitation by prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Notably, the carbon source itself dictated the organism's denitrification behavior, switching it between distinct regulatory strategies. By resolving these mechanisms in a single isolate, this work clarifies how facultative denitrifiers may process depolymerized plant carbon and shape nitrogen gas emissions in oxygen-limited environments, and identifies traits relevant to the downstream microbial valorization of lignin-derived aromatics.

records.title: Diagnosing pediatric skeletal system infections: you are as good as your lab.
records.abstract: Pediatric skeletal system infections are medical emergencies that may cause severe acute complications and long-term orthopedic disabilities. Because the clinical presentation of septic arthritis and osteomyelitis may mimic non-infectious conditions, early identification of the causative agent and determination of its antibiotic susceptibility profile are cornerstones of patient management. The etiology of childhood skeletal system infections has changed over time, reflecting the implementation of conjugate vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae, as well as the development of sensitive molecular detection tests. These novel laboratory methods, coupled with rapid pathogen identification by MALDI-TOF technology, have reduced the fraction of "culture-negative" infections and shortened the turnaround time for pathogen identification from days to hours. However, even today, a substantial fraction of bone and joint infections remains microbiologically unconfirmed. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing holds great promise, but its high cost, the need for technical expertise, and the detection of commensal organisms of dubious significance severely limit its routine use. On the other hand, metagenomic next-generation sequencing has not expanded the list of known pediatric skeletal system pathogens, suggesting that underutilization of current diagnostic methodologies, rather than reduced sensitivity, drives suboptimal diagnosis.
records.authors: Yagupsky P.

records.title: Characterization of clinical isolates of Acinetobacter baumannii and comparative proteomic profiling among strong and weak biofilm formers.
records.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii, a critical priority pathogen, is also notable for its biofilm-forming abilities on medical devices like ventilators, catheters, and surgical drain tubes. The biofilm formation causes increased tolerance against antibiotics, making treatment difficult. The clinical isolates of A. baumannii present varied biofilm-forming capacity; hence, understanding the molecular determinants responsible for strong biofilm is crucial. The present study aims to characterize the antibiotic and biofilm-forming profile of 25 clinical isolates of A. baumannii and compare the proteome profiling of strong and weak biofilm-forming isolates to identify therapeutic targets. We observed n = 23 of the isolates as multidrug resistant, and n = 13 were forming strong biofilms. Comparative proteomic profiling revealed 42 differentially regulated proteins. In the strong biofilm-forming isolate new lipoprotein A (NLPA), uL16, DNA gyrase B, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and purL were found to be upregulated, highlighting a dynamic reprogramming of cellular functions that promotes biofilm formation, stress adaptation, and immune evasion. In contrast, EF-Tu, ribosome hibernation factors, and T6SS components were downregulated, suggesting a lack of biosynthesis and cellular adaptability. These findings suggest a metabolic downshift and a possible energy conservation mechanism under conditions less favorable for strong biofilm development. Additionally, several uncharacterized proteins were identified, highlighting potential novel factors in biofilm regulation and virulence that warrant further investigation. The proteomics data correlated with qPCR findings, providing support for the unknown regulators of biofilm formation that were identified in this study. Key proteins, such as NLPA, 6,7-dimethyl-8-ribityllumazine synthase, and DNA gyrase B emerged as potential therapeutic targets that may be used for drug discovery.ImportanceAcinetobacter baumannii has progressively evolved into a serious cause of both hospital and community-acquired infections. This bacterium's resilience to harsh conditions, bacterial dormancy within biofilms, antibiotic resistance, and survival on inanimate surfaces contribute to its ability to cause chronic, hard-to-eradicate infections. The molecular determinants underlying variations in biofilm-forming capacity among clinical isolates remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses this gap by identifying key molecular adaptations associated with strong biofilm formation. By uncovering pathways linked to biofilm persistence, this work provides valuable insights into bacterial survival strategies and highlights potential avenues for therapeutic intervention. These findings lay the groundwork for the development of new anti-biofilm strategies aimed at improving treatment outcomes and combating antimicrobial resistance.

records.title: VarNexus: an integrative database for interpreting disease-associated regulatory variants through multimodal predictions and functional evidence.
records.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous loci associated with complex diseases and traits, yet the functional interpretation of non-coding risk variants remains challenging. Sequence-to-function models like AlphaGenome provide large-scale multi-modal predictions of variant effects, but their predictions lack direct experimental support. In contrast, empirical resources such as molecular quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) offer population-based or experimental support for variant function, but suffer from limited genomic coverage. Here, we present VarNexus (https://biomed.imu.edu.cn/varnexus), an integrative resource for connecting disease-associated variants with predicted, population-based, and experimental evidence. VarNexus currently contains 230 404 fine-mapped candidate variants across 1891 disease-related phenotypes from UK Biobank and FinnGen. It integrates precomputed AlphaGenome predictions across 11 regulatory output types with bulk and single-cell xQTLs, MPRA measurements, and GWAS-eQTL colocalization results. VarNexus enables cross-linked searches by variant, phenotype, and gene, together with on-demand AlphaGenome prediction, multi-omics genome-browser visualization, and regulatory network exploration. By combining sequence-based predictions with population-based and experimental evidence, VarNexus provides a framework for prioritizing candidate regulatory mechanisms supported by multiple evidence layers.
records.authors: Gong L, Tan C, Zhang J, Shu R, Guo S, Xiao T, Shi J, Wang J, Ni T, Ding R.

records.title: Inhibition of malignant progression in mesenchymal glioblastoma by PARP1 inhibitors.
records.abstract: BackgroundAmong molecular subtypes of glioblastoma (GBM), the mesenchymal subtype (MES) exhibits the most aggressive clinical course, marked by heightened invasiveness and therapeutic resistance. To overcome the challenge of intrinsic drug resistance in MES GBM, we performed a high-throughput screen of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells.MethodsWe performed a high-throughput screen of 2,697 FDA-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells, engineered via CRISPR/Cas9.ResultsThis screen nominated poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) inhibitors as top candidates, demonstrating selective cytotoxicity against NF1-deficient cells. Integrated analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data, immunofluorescence, and immunoblotting revealed significant PARP1 upregulation in GBM tissues, establishing its role as a proto-oncogene that drives tumor cell proliferation and migration. Using orthotopic xenograft models, we confirmed that NF1 knockdown (KD) profoundly sensitized GBM tumors to the anti-tumor and pro-apoptotic effects of PARP1 inhibition in vivo. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays identified a physical interaction between the NF1 gene product neurofibromin and PARP1, suggesting a direct regulatory nexus.ConclusionsThis study breaks through the traditional limitation of PARP inhibitors being used only for DNA repair defects, and for the first time reveals a novel selective killing mechanism of PARP1 inhibitors in NF1-deficient GBM. Collectively, our findings delineate NF1-mutant, MES GBM as a distinct clinical subset poised to derive therapeutic benefit from PARP1-targeted therapy.
records.authors: Zhang H, Li Q, Yao X, Wang B, Pan Y, Yuan G.

records.title: Thermal stress suppresses methanogenesis while Fe(III) alters carbon-related responses during microplastic aging in landfill leachate.
records.abstract: Landfill leachate differs from many anaerobic aquatic environments because it combines darkness, oxygen limitation, high dissolved organic matter, reactive iron, plastic contamination, high ionic strength, and localized heat stress. These conditions may precondition microplastics (MPs), but whether MP aging in leachate promotes anaerobic greenhouse-gas production remains unclear. Here, polyethylene (PE), polystyrene (PS), and polylactic acid (PLA) MPs were incubated for 90 d in field-collected landfill leachate at 30 °C or 70 °C, with or without Fe(III) amendment. Temperature dominated the measured carbon-related responses: compared with 30 °C, 70 °C reduced headspace CO2C accumulation from 2.0 to 3.8 to 0.1-1.1 mg C and eliminated detectable headspace CH4. Under thermal stress, Fe(III) addition was associated with greater DOC depletion, lower filter-passing Fe concentrations, and increased filter-retained solid-phase C. MP aging was polymer dependent: PE mainly served as a scaffold for Fe-DOM coating, PS showed Fe-sensitive carbonyl-region changes and localized deposits, and PLA exhibited hydrolysis-associated disruption. Heat stress reduced microbial diversity and strongly diminished methanogenesis-associated archaea, whereas putative polymer-associated ASVs remained embedded within Fe-regulated and polymer-specific environments. These findings highlight polymer-specific surface alteration and concurrent changes in carbon fractions under thermal stress and Fe(III) amendment, with temperature exerting the dominant constraint on methanogenesis in the tested leachate system.
records.authors: Zhao Z, Fu Y, Pan Z, Bao LJ, Dang F, Zhou F, Zhai X, Zhu X, Wang X, Pan X, Fang M, Wang Z.

records.title: DnaK1-mediated regulation of phototactic motility in Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 3055.
records.abstract: Cyanobacterial phototaxis relies on type IV pili (T4P); yet, how light signals are transmitted to the T4P motor remains unresolved. Here, we identify the molecular chaperone DnaK1 as an important regulator of phototactic motility in Synechococcus elongatus UTEX 3055. DnaK1 interacts with the phototaxis regulator PixGSe and the T4P extension ATPase PilB, and loss of dnaK1 impairs phototactic motility. Mutations in dnaJ1 impair phototaxis, and a partially segregated grpE mutant shows a similar but milder defect, suggesting that the DnaK1-DnaJ1-GrpE system may contribute to this process. Fluorescence imaging shows that DnaK1, PixGSe, and PilB have similar polar localization patterns. Based on these findings, we propose a working model in which DnaK1 may facilitate the assembly or stability of phototaxis-associated T4P complexes, thereby providing a potential mechanistic link between the phototaxis signaling module and T4P motor activity. These findings establish a link between DnaK1 and the phototaxis machinery, highlighting a potential role for molecular chaperones in coupling light-sensing pathways to T4P-mediated motility.
records.authors: Li SY, Sun QX, Huang DQ, Xie T, Yu Y, He C, Valades-Cruz CA, Zeng X, Yang Y, Zhang CC.

records.title: Gene-radon interaction effects on lung cancer risk: validation of susceptibility loci using archived DNA from German Uranium miners.
records.abstract: BackgroundRadon exposure increases lung cancer risk, shown in studies on indoor exposure (low exposure) and uranium miners (high exposure). Genome-wide and candidate gene studies have identified DNA variants that interact with occupational radon to modify lung cancer risk.MethodHighly fragmented DNA samples of 611 individuals were genotyped using next-generation sequencing. DNA variant associations could be assessed in 526 out of 611 WISMUT uranium miners with lung cancer. The relative risk of lung cancer per allele (marginal effect) as well as its dependence on radon exposure (gene-environment (GxE) interaction) could be estimated from the enrichment of one allele compared to the distribution of genotypes expected under the HWE assumption (Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium). Exposure to gamma radiation, long-lived radionuclides, fine dust, silicate dust and arsenic was considered in the same way.ResultsFor markers from six (UBE2U, CDKN2A, SIRT1, NAV2, ST8SIA2, TP53) of the 10 genes examined, a significant modification of the genetic relative risk for lung cancer due to mining-specific radon exposure [in WLM] was observed.ConclusionRadon exposure may be the main cause of some of the observed GxE interactions involving UBE2U, CDKN2A and SIRT1, but it may not be the only one. This conclusion is supported by the function of these genes, as based on relevant literature. For another marker of the gene SOX5, a GxE interaction can presumably be attributed to exposure to arsenic. For the remaining genes, no single environmental factor (radon, dust or arsenic) can unambiguously be identified as sole cause of the GxE interaction.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.
records.journal: Genes and environment : the official journal of the Japanese Environmental Mutagen Society
records.authors: Rosenberger A, Bonzheim I, Fend F, Hochstrat B, Johnen G, Brik A, Rozynek P, Bickeböller H, Mörtl S, Gomolka M.
